↓
<h1>Q35 · Scaphoid Fracture / Anatomic Snuffbox</h1>
↓
<strong>What Step 1 is testing:</strong> FOOSH + anatomic snuffbox tenderness = <strong>scaphoid fracture</strong> (most commonly fractured carpal bone).

[20-year-old + fall on outstretched hand + snuffbox tenderness]

➔ Scaphoid fracture

➔ Most commonly fractured carpal bone

➔ Complication: avascular necrosis (retrograde blood supply)

➔ ✅ A. Scaphoid

> 💡 <strong>Step 1 Rule:</strong> <strong>Snuffbox tenderness after FOOSH = scaphoid until proven otherwise.</strong> Even if initial X-ray is negative, treat empirically (thumb spica cast) and repeat imaging in 2 weeks. The scaphoid has a <strong>retrograde blood supply</strong> (distal → proximal), so fractures of the proximal pole risk <strong>avascular necrosis</strong>. The NBME loves testing this complication.
↓
<h1>Q36 · Nerve Regeneration / Slow Anterograde Axonal Transport</h1>
↓
<strong>What Step 1 is testing:</strong> After peripheral nerve injury, which transport process is rate-limiting for regeneration?

[C-section → numbness around incision → nerves regenerating]

➔ Peripheral nerve transection → Wallerian degeneration distally

➔ Regeneration requires:

1. Retrograde signaling to cell body (injury signals)

2. Cell body response (chromatolysis, ↑ protein synthesis)

3. Slow anterograde transport of cytoskeletal proteins for axon regrowth

➔ Rate-limiting step for RETURN TO NORMAL SENSATION = slow anterograde transport

(axon regrows at ~1-3 mm/day = rate of slow axonal transport)

➔ ✅ E. Slow anterograde axonal transport

<strong>Note:</strong> The provided answer key lists D (retrograde) as correct, emphasizing that retrograde signaling initiates the cell body response. However, the standard Step 1 teaching is that <strong>slow anterograde transport</strong> (~1 mm/day) determines the rate of physical axon regrowth and is the rate-limiting step for functional recovery. This is a commonly debated question — know both perspectives.
↓
> 💡 <strong>Step 1 Rule:</strong> Peripheral nerve regeneration rate ≈ <strong>1 mm/day</strong> (or ~1 inch/month), which corresponds to the rate of <strong>slow anterograde axonal transport</strong> of cytoskeletal proteins (neurofilaments, tubulin). This is why recovery takes weeks to months depending on the distance from injury to target.
↓
<h1>Q37 · Tamoxifen / Competitive ER Antagonist</h1>
↓
<strong>What Step 1 is testing:</strong> Tamoxifen = SERM = <strong>competitive inhibitor</strong> of estradiol binding to its receptor in breast tissue.

[70-year-old + breast cancer 5 years ago + on tamoxifen → no recurrence]

➔ Tamoxifen = Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM)

➔ ANTAGONIST in breast (blocks ER → ↓ tumor growth)

➔ AGONIST in bone (↑ BMD) and endometrium (↑ endometrial cancer risk)

➔ Mechanism: competitive inhibition of estradiol binding to ER

➔ ✅ B. Competitive inhibition of estradiol binding to its receptor

<strong>Key SERM distinctions for Step 1:</strong>
↓

↓
> 💡 <strong>Step 1 Rule:</strong> Tamoxifen <strong>competes</strong> with estradiol for the ER — it's a competitive antagonist in breast tissue. Don't confuse with: aromatase inhibitors (block estrogen SYNTHESIS), fulvestrant (DOWNREGULATES ER), or GnRH agonists (suppress gonadotropins).
↓
<h1>Q38 · Sickle Cell / Renal Papillary Necrosis</h1>
↓
<strong>What Step 1 is testing:</strong> Sickle cell disease → medullary ischemia → renal papillary necrosis → hematuria + flank pain.

[24-year-old with sickle cell crisis → sudden hematuria + flank pain]

➔ Renal papillary necrosis (RPN)

➔ Sickle cells occlude vasa recta → medullary ischemia → papillary infarction

➔ Sloughed papillae → hematuria, flank pain, possible ureteral obstruction

➔ ✅ D. Renal papillary necrosis

<strong>Causes of RPN — mnemonic: "SAND"</strong>
↓
<strong>S</strong>ickle cell disease
↓
<strong>A</strong>nalgesics (NSAIDs, phenacetin)
↓
<strong>N</strong>ephritis (acute pyelonephritis)
↓
<strong>D</strong>iabetes mellitus
↓
> 💡 <strong>Step 1 Rule:</strong> Sickle cell + hematuria + flank pain = <strong>renal papillary necrosis</strong>. The renal medulla is particularly vulnerable in SCD because it's already hypoxic and hypertonic — perfect conditions for sickling. Don't pick glomerulonephritis (would have RBC casts) or nephrolithiasis (less specific to SCD).
↓
<h1>Q39 · Laryngeal Papillomatosis / HPV</h1>
↓
<strong>What Step 1 is testing:</strong> Finger-like excrescences on vocal cords in an infant = <strong>laryngeal papillomatosis</strong> from vertical transmission of <strong>HPV</strong> (types 6 and 11).

[2-month-old + noisy/difficult breathing + slender finger-like growths on vocal cords]

➔ Laryngeal papillomatosis

➔ Caused by HPV types 6 and 11 (low-risk, same as genital warts)

➔ Vertical transmission during passage through infected birth canal

➔ ✅ D. Human papillomavirus

> 💡 <strong>Step 1 Rule:</strong> Papillomas (finger-like/warty growths) in a neonate = <strong>HPV 6/11</strong> from maternal transmission. Don't confuse with HSV (vesicles, encephalitis) or Chlamydia (conjunctivitis, pneumonia). HPV 6/11 = warts/papillomas (benign). HPV 16/18 = dysplasia/cancer (malignant).

[70-year-old + CABG/AVR + post-op BP 80/40 → required pressors]

➔ 24 hours later: Cr 4.5 (baseline 1.0), urine output 15 mL/hr

➔ Prolonged hypotension → renal hypoperfusion → ischemic ATN

➔ Muddy brown casts, FENa >2%, BUN:Cr <20

➔ ✅ B. Acute tubular necrosis from ischemia

Unconjugated bilirubin is lipid-soluble → crosses BBB
↓
Causes: hemolytic disease of newborn (Rh/ABO incompatibility), G6PD, physiologic jaundice (severe)
↓
Biliary atresia = CONJUGATED → water-soluble → does NOT cross BBB → NO kernicterus
↓
✅ C. Hemolytic disease of the newborn

Why each distractor fails:
• (A) Biliary atresia — Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Cannot cause kernicterus. This is the #1 trap.
• (B) Cyanotic CHD — Does not cause severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia
• (D) Neonatal meningitis — Purulent exudate, not yellow pigment staining
• (E) RDS — Causes hyaline membranes, germinal matrix hemorrhage — not kernicterus

💡 Step 1 Rule: Kernicterus = unconjugated bilirubin ONLY. Conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and cannot cross the BBB. If you see yellow basal ganglia at autopsy, the bilirubin was unconjugated → hemolysis.

nbme28_q0135.title: DiGeorge Syndrome / Microdeletion
nbme28_q0135.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: DiGeorge = 22q11.2 microdeletion — too small for standard karyotype → normal 46,XX but abnormal on FISH.

MetricValue
Core ConceptMicrodeletion at 22q11.2 — submicroscopic, normal karyotype, requires FISH to detect
DifficultyMedium
HY LevelTier 1 — Genetics (Microdeletion syndromes)
TrapThe question says karyotype is "normal 46,XX" — students think "can't be a deletion if karyotype is normal"
[Infant: cyanosis + tetralogy of Fallot + hypocalcemia + lymphopenia]
↓
CATCH-22: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia → 22q11.2
↓
Karyotype: 46,XX (normal) — because deletion is SUBMICROSCOPIC
↓
Detected by FISH or chromosomal microarray, NOT standard G-banding
↓
Genetic mechanism = DELETION (microdeletion)
↓
✅ A. Deletion

Why each distractor fails:
• (B) Nondisjunction — Produces aneuploidy (47,XX+21) → abnormal chromosome COUNT
• (C–D) Inversions — Structural rearrangements, not the mechanism of DiGeorge
• (E–F) Translocations — Would be visible on karyotype
• (G) Trinucleotide repeat — Fragile X, Huntington, myotonic dystrophy
• (H) Uniparental disomy — Prader-Willi/Angelman mechanism

💡 Step 1 Rule: Normal karyotype + clinical syndrome = microdeletion (too small for G-banding). DiGeorge (22q11.2), Williams (7q11.23), Cri-du-chat (5p). Detect with FISH or microarray.

nbme29_q0170.title: Beckwith-Wiedemann / Imprinting
nbme29_q0170.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Abnormal methylation at a differentially methylated region (DMR) on a specific parental allele = genomic imprinting.

MetricValue
Core ConceptGenomic imprinting — gene expression depends on parental origin via DNA methylation
DifficultyMedium–Hard
HY LevelTier 1 — Genetics (Epigenetics/Imprinting)
TrapPicking pleiotropy — BWS does affect multiple organs, but the question asks about the GENETIC MECHANISM (abnormal methylation at DMR2)
[Macrosomia + macroglossia + nevus flammeus + Wilms tumor + abnormal methylation at 11p15]
↓
Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
↓
Abnormal methylation at KCNQ1OT1 (DMR2) on MATERNAL allele
↓
Expression depends on PARENTAL ORIGIN = IMPRINTING
↓
✅ C. Imprinting

Key imprinting disorders for Step 1:

DisorderLocusMechanismFeatures
Prader-Willi15q11-13Loss of PATERNAL alleleHypotonia, obesity, hypogonadism, intellectual disability
Angelman15q11-13Loss of MATERNAL allele"Happy puppet," seizures, ataxia, inappropriate laughter
Beckwith-Wiedemann11p15.5Abnormal methylation of MATERNAL alleleMacrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele, Wilms tumor
💡 Step 1 Rule: If the question mentions abnormal methylation at a differentially methylated region on a specific parental allele → the answer is imprinting. Don't get distracted by pleiotropy (one gene, many effects) — that's a different concept.

nbme28_q0104.title: Abetalipoproteinemia / Apo B Deficiency
nbme28_q0104.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Can you connect acanthocytes + fat malabsorption + very low cholesterol + neurologic findings to a lipoprotein assembly defect?

MetricValue
Core ConceptApo B deficiency → can't assemble chylomicrons/VLDL → fat malabsorption, acanthocytes, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
DifficultyMedium
HY LevelTier 1 — Biochemistry (Lipoproteins)
TrapPicking Apo E (dysbetalipoproteinemia) — that causes HIGH cholesterol, not LOW
[Intellectual disability + retinitis pigmentosa + acanthocytes + cholesterol 40 mg/dL + chronic diarrhea + ataxia]
↓
Abetalipoproteinemia (Bassen-Kornzweig syndrome)
↓
Defective Apo B → can't form chylomicrons or VLDL
↓
Fat trapped in enterocytes → steatorrhea
↓
↓ Fat-soluble vitamins (A → night blindness, E → neuro degeneration, K → bleeding)
↓
Altered RBC membrane lipids → acanthocytes (spiny RBCs)
↓
✅ C. Apo B

Distractor logic:
• Apo A-I — HDL structural protein. Deficiency → low HDL, CV risk. Not this picture.
• Apo C-II — Activates LPL. Deficiency → hypertriglyceridemia (opposite problem).
• Apo E — Hepatic uptake of remnants. Deficiency → type III hyperlipoproteinemia.

💡 Step 1 Rule: Acanthocytes + very low cholesterol + fat malabsorption + retinitis pigmentosa = abetalipoproteinemia (Apo B deficiency). The neurologic findings are from vitamin E deficiency. The night blindness is from vitamin A deficiency.

nbme29_q0002.title: Gag Reflex / CN IX Afferent
nbme29_q0002.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Afferent vs. efferent limbs of the gag reflex — CN IX (sensory) vs. CN X (motor).

[Bronchoscopy → anesthetize pharynx to prevent gag]
↓
Gag reflex: Afferent = CN IX (glossopharyngeal), Efferent = CN X (vagus)
↓
Anesthesia blocks the AFFERENT (sensory) limb
↓
✅ C. Glossopharyngeal
💡 Step 1 Rule: Gag reflex = 9 senses it, 10 acts on it. CN IX = afferent (posterior pharynx sensation). CN X = efferent (pharyngeal constrictor contraction). The NBME always asks which limb is blocked by anesthesia — that's the afferent = CN IX.

form30_page-101.title: Allergic Rhinitis / Eosinophils in Nasal Secretions
form30_page-101.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Type I hypersensitivity → late-phase reaction → eosinophil recruitment.

[Seasonal sneezing, nasal stuffiness, watery eyes while gardening]
↓
Allergic rhinitis = Type I hypersensitivity (IgE-mediated)
↓
Early phase: mast cell degranulation → histamine
↓
Late phase: EOSINOPHIL recruitment to nasal mucosa
↓
Eosinophils = hallmark cell in nasal secretions of allergic rhinitis
↓
✅ B. Eosinophils

Why not mast cells (D)? Mast cells are tissue-resident — they degranulate in place but are not found increased in secretions. Eosinophils are recruited to the site and appear in the nasal discharge.

💡 Step 1 Rule: Allergic inflammation → eosinophils are the recruited effector cells. Mast cells start the reaction (early phase), eosinophils sustain it (late phase). In nasal secretions, blood, or tissue of allergic disease → look for eosinophils.

metrics.mostCommonWrong: D (Mast cells) — tissue-bound, not in secretions

form30_page-111.title: Thyroid Scan / T₄ Bound to TBG
form30_page-111.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Most circulating thyroid hormone is T₄ (not T₃), and most T₄ is bound to TBG (not transthyretin or albumin).

[¹²³I thyroid scan → 1 week later → where is most circulating ¹²³I?]
↓
¹²³I incorporated into newly synthesized thyroid hormone
↓
Thyroid secretes ~90% T₄, ~10% T₃
↓
>99% of T₄ is protein-bound: TBG (~70%) > transthyretin (~15%) > albumin (~15%)
↓
Largest pool = T₄ bound to TBG
↓
✅ E. T₄ bound to T₄-binding globulin
💡 Step 1 Rule: T₄ is the major secreted hormone. TBG is the major binding protein. Therefore, the largest circulating pool of iodine = T₄ bound to TBG. Free T₄ is only ~0.03% of total. Don't pick free hormone — it's biologically active but quantitatively tiny.

metrics.mostCommonWrong: D/F (T₄ bound to transthyretin) — minor carrier

form30_page-147.title: HOCM / Dynamic Outflow Obstruction
form30_page-147.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: HOCM murmur dynamics — increases with ↓ preload (Valsalva, standing), decreases with ↑ preload (squatting, leg elevation).

MetricValue
Core ConceptHOCM = asymmetric septal hypertrophy → dynamic LVOT obstruction → murmur changes with preload
DifficultyMedium
HY LevelTier 1 — Cardiology (Murmur dynamics)
TrapPicking aortic stenosis — also systolic, but AS murmur DECREASES with Valsalva (less flow across valve)
[Young athlete + syncope during exercise + systolic murmur at LLSB]
↓
Murmur ↑ with Valsalva (↓ preload → smaller LV → more obstruction)
↓
Murmur ↓ with leg elevation (↑ preload → larger LV → less obstruction)
↓
= HOCM (dynamic obstruction)
↓
✅ C. Idiopathic hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy

The critical distinction — HOCM vs. everything else:

ManeuverHOCM MurmurMost Other Murmurs (AS, MR, VSD)
Valsalva / Standing (↓ preload)LOUDERSofter
Squatting / Leg elevation (↑ preload)SOFTERLouder
💡 Step 1 Rule: HOCM is the ONLY murmur that gets LOUDER with Valsalva. Everything else gets softer. If the vignette says "murmur increases with strain/standing and decreases with squatting/leg elevation" → HOCM. Young athlete + syncope + family history of sudden death = classic setup.

form31_page-15.title: Obstructive Uropathy / Compensated Metabolic Acidosis
form31_page-15.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Can you apply Winter's formula to identify appropriately compensated metabolic acidosis?

[BPH → bilateral hydronephrosis → AKI → metabolic acidosis]
↓
Obstructive uropathy → type IV RTA / impaired H⁺ secretion → metabolic acidosis
↓
HCO₃⁻ = 15 → Winter's formula: expected PCO₂ = 1.5(15) + 8 ± 2 = 28.5–32.5
↓
Option B: pH 7.32, PCO₂ 30, HCO₃⁻ 15 → PCO₂ matches Winter's prediction ✅
↓
= Appropriately compensated metabolic acidosis
↓
✅ B

Why each distractor fails:
• (A) PCO₂ 44 with HCO₃⁻ 18 → PCO₂ too HIGH (expected ~35) → concurrent respiratory acidosis
• (C) Normal ABG — doesn't reflect the AKI
• (D, E) Metabolic alkalosis patterns — opposite direction
• (F) Primary respiratory alkalosis — no metabolic acidosis component

💡 Step 1 Rule: Winter's formula: Expected PCO₂ = 1.5 × [HCO₃⁻] + 8 ± 2. If the actual PCO₂ matches → appropriately compensated metabolic acidosis. If PCO₂ is higher than predicted → concurrent respiratory acidosis. If lower → concurrent respiratory alkalosis.

form31_page-5.title: Marfan Syndrome / Aortic Insufficiency
form31_page-5.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Marfan → cystic medial degeneration → aortic root dilation → aortic regurgitation (diastolic murmur).

[Tall, thin woman + joint hypermobility + pectus excavatum + NEW DIASTOLIC murmur]
↓
Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1 mutation → FBN1)
↓
Cystic medial degeneration of aorta → aortic root dilation
↓
Dilated aortic root → aortic valve can't coapt → regurgitation
↓
Aortic regurgitation = DIASTOLIC decrescendo murmur
↓
✅ A. Aortic insufficiency

Why not mitral regurgitation (C)? MR is a systolic murmur, not diastolic. While Marfan can cause mitral valve prolapse, the question specifies a new diastolic murmur → aortic regurgitation.

💡 Step 1 Rule: Marfan + new diastolic murmur = aortic regurgitation from aortic root dilation. Marfan triad: (1) tall/arachnodactyly, (2) lens subluxation (UP and OUT), (3) aortic root dilation/dissection. The diastolic murmur is the cardiovascular complication they test most.

form31_page-124.title: PID / Neisseria gonorrhoeae
form31_page-124.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: PID in a young woman → #1 cause = N. gonorrhoeae (or Chlamydia trachomatis).

[24-year-old + fever + lower abdominal pain + onset during menses + tubal/ovarian tenderness + leukocytosis]
↓
Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID)
↓
Most common causes: N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis
↓
Onset during menses = classic (cervical os open → ascending infection)
↓
✅ B. Neisseria gonorrhoeae

Why not the others?
• Gardnerella — Bacterial vaginosis (fishy discharge), does NOT ascend to cause PID
• S. aureus — Skin infections, TSS, not typical PID pathogen
• GBS — Peripartum pathogen, not PID
• Trichomonas — Vaginitis (frothy discharge), does NOT cause PID

💡 Step 1 Rule: PID = ascending infection from cervix → uterus → tubes → ovaries. Top two organisms: N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. Onset during menstruation is a classic board clue (open cervical os facilitates ascent). Complication: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis (perihepatitis with "violin string" adhesions).

nbme27_page-101.title: Valproic Acid / Histone Deacetylase → Transcription
nbme27_page-101.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: HDAC inhibition → ↑ histone acetylation → open chromatin → ↑ transcription.

[Bipolar disorder → valproic acid → inhibits histone deacetylase]
↓
HDAC inhibition → acetyl groups STAY on histones
↓
Acetylated histones → loose chromatin (euchromatin)
↓
DNA more accessible to transcription factors
↓
↑ TRANSCRIPTION
↓
✅ D. Transcription

The epigenetics logic:

ModificationChromatin StateEffect on Transcription
Acetylation (by HATs)Open (euchromatin)↑ Transcription
Deacetylation (by HDACs)Closed (heterochromatin)↓ Transcription
Methylation (DNA)Usually closedUsually ↓ Transcription
💡 Step 1 Rule: Acetylation = Activation of transcription. HDAC removes acetyl groups → silences genes. HDAC inhibitors (like valproate) keep acetyl groups on → genes stay active → ↑ transcription. The downstream steps (splicing, polyadenylation, translation) are NOT directly affected by chromatin remodeling.

nbme27_page-139.title: Aortic Stenosis / Congenital Bicuspid Valve
nbme27_page-139.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Age of presentation determines the etiology of aortic stenosis.

[52-year-old + exertional syncope/dyspnea/angina + systolic murmur at RUSB + pressure gradient LV > Aorta]
↓
Aortic stenosis
↓
Age 40–60 → BICUSPID AORTIC VALVE (congenital, accelerated calcification)
↓
Age >60 → Degenerative calcific (senile) aortic stenosis
↓
Young adult in developing country → Rheumatic heart disease
↓
✅ A. Congenital bicuspid valve
Age of AS PresentationMost Likely Etiology
< 30Unicuspid or severely malformed valve
40–60Bicuspid aortic valve (most common congenital cardiac anomaly)
> 60–70Degenerative calcific (senile)
Any age (developing world)Rheumatic heart disease
💡 Step 1 Rule: The NBME uses age to determine AS etiology. Patient in their 50s with AS = bicuspid valve. Patient in their 70s–80s = degenerative/senile calcification. Bicuspid valve is the most common congenital cardiac anomaly (~1–2% of population) and causes premature calcification.

nbme27_page-14.title: Kaposi Sarcoma / Spindle Cells with Slit-Like Spaces
nbme27_page-14.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: HIV + violaceous plaques → Kaposi sarcoma → HHV-8 → histology = spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces.

[34-year-old HIV+ man + violaceous raised plaques]
↓
Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8)
↓
Histology: proliferating SPINDLE CELLS forming SLIT-LIKE SPACES filled with blood
↓
✅ E

Distractor histology decoder:
• (A) Dense acellular fibrous tissue → Scar/fibromatosis
• (B) Large polygonal cells with myofibrils → Rhabdomyosarcoma
• (C) Malignant glands with mucin → Adenocarcinoma
• (D) Poorly differentiated squamous cells → Squamous cell carcinoma

💡 Step 1 Rule: HIV + purple skin lesions = Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8). The pathognomonic histology is spindle cells with slit-like vascular spaces. It's a vascular tumor — the slits are abnormal blood-filled channels.

nbme28_q0016.title: Scaphoid Fracture / Anatomic Snuffbox
nbme28_q0016.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: FOOSH + anatomic snuffbox tenderness = scaphoid fracture (most commonly fractured carpal bone).

[20-year-old + fall on outstretched hand + snuffbox tenderness]
↓
Scaphoid fracture
↓
Most commonly fractured carpal bone
↓
Complication: avascular necrosis (retrograde blood supply)
↓
✅ A. Scaphoid
💡 Step 1 Rule: Snuffbox tenderness after FOOSH = scaphoid until proven otherwise. Even if initial X-ray is negative, treat empirically (thumb spica cast) and repeat imaging in 2 weeks. The scaphoid has a retrograde blood supply (distal → proximal), so fractures of the proximal pole risk avascular necrosis. The NBME loves testing this complication.

nbme28_q0054.title: Nerve Regeneration / Slow Anterograde Axonal Transport
nbme28_q0054.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: After peripheral nerve injury, which transport process is rate-limiting for regeneration?

[C-section → numbness around incision → nerves regenerating]
↓
Peripheral nerve transection → Wallerian degeneration distally
↓
Regeneration requires:
↓
1. Retrograde signaling to cell body (injury signals)
↓
2. Cell body response (chromatolysis, ↑ protein synthesis)
↓
3. Slow anterograde transport of cytoskeletal proteins for axon regrowth
↓
Rate-limiting step for RETURN TO NORMAL SENSATION = slow anterograde transport
↓
(axon regrows at ~1-3 mm/day = rate of slow axonal transport)
↓
✅ E. Slow anterograde axonal transport

Note: The provided answer key lists D (retrograde) as correct, emphasizing that retrograde signaling initiates the cell body response. However, the standard Step 1 teaching is that slow anterograde transport (~1 mm/day) determines the rate of physical axon regrowth and is the rate-limiting step for functional recovery. This is a commonly debated question — know both perspectives.

💡 Step 1 Rule: Peripheral nerve regeneration rate ≈ 1 mm/day (or ~1 inch/month), which corresponds to the rate of slow anterograde axonal transport of cytoskeletal proteins (neurofilaments, tubulin). This is why recovery takes weeks to months depending on the distance from injury to target.

metrics.mostCommonWrong: E (Slow anterograde) — determines axon growth speed

nbme29_q0005.title: Tamoxifen / Competitive ER Antagonist
nbme29_q0005.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Tamoxifen = SERM = competitive inhibitor of estradiol binding to its receptor in breast tissue.

[70-year-old + breast cancer 5 years ago + on tamoxifen → no recurrence]
↓
Tamoxifen = Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM)
↓
ANTAGONIST in breast (blocks ER → ↓ tumor growth)
↓
AGONIST in bone (↑ BMD) and endometrium (↑ endometrial cancer risk)
↓
Mechanism: competitive inhibition of estradiol binding to ER
↓
✅ B. Competitive inhibition of estradiol binding to its receptor

Key SERM distinctions for Step 1:

DrugBreastBoneEndometriumClinical Use
TamoxifenAntagonist ✅AgonistAgonist (↑ cancer risk)ER+ breast cancer
RaloxifeneAntagonist ✅AgonistAntagonist (no ↑ risk)Osteoporosis prevention
ClomipheneAntagonist (hypothalamus)——Ovulation induction
💡 Step 1 Rule: Tamoxifen competes with estradiol for the ER — it's a competitive antagonist in breast tissue. Don't confuse with: aromatase inhibitors (block estrogen SYNTHESIS), fulvestrant (DOWNREGULATES ER), or GnRH agonists (suppress gonadotropins).

form30_page-73.title: Sickle Cell / Renal Papillary Necrosis
form30_page-73.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Sickle cell disease → medullary ischemia → renal papillary necrosis → hematuria + flank pain.

[24-year-old with sickle cell crisis → sudden hematuria + flank pain]
↓
Renal papillary necrosis (RPN)
↓
Sickle cells occlude vasa recta → medullary ischemia → papillary infarction
↓
Sloughed papillae → hematuria, flank pain, possible ureteral obstruction
↓
✅ D. Renal papillary necrosis

Causes of RPN — mnemonic: "SAND"
• Sickle cell disease
• Analgesics (NSAIDs, phenacetin)
• Nephritis (acute pyelonephritis)
• Diabetes mellitus

💡 Step 1 Rule: Sickle cell + hematuria + flank pain = renal papillary necrosis. The renal medulla is particularly vulnerable in SCD because it's already hypoxic and hypertonic — perfect conditions for sickling. Don't pick glomerulonephritis (would have RBC casts) or nephrolithiasis (less specific to SCD).

form31_page-31.title: Laryngeal Papillomatosis / HPV
form31_page-31.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Finger-like excrescences on vocal cords in an infant = laryngeal papillomatosis from vertical transmission of HPV (types 6 and 11).

[2-month-old + noisy/difficult breathing + slender finger-like growths on vocal cords]
↓
Laryngeal papillomatosis
↓
Caused by HPV types 6 and 11 (low-risk, same as genital warts)
↓
Vertical transmission during passage through infected birth canal
↓
✅ D. Human papillomavirus
💡 Step 1 Rule: Papillomas (finger-like/warty growths) in a neonate = HPV 6/11 from maternal transmission. Don't confuse with HSV (vesicles, encephalitis) or Chlamydia (conjunctivitis, pneumonia). HPV 6/11 = warts/papillomas (benign). HPV 16/18 = dysplasia/cancer (malignant).

nbme27_page-109.title: Post-Cardiac Surgery AKI / Ischemic ATN
nbme27_page-109.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Prolonged hypotension → ischemic acute tubular necrosis (intrinsic renal failure).

[70-year-old + CABG/AVR + post-op BP 80/40 → required pressors]
↓
24 hours later: Cr 4.5 (baseline 1.0), urine output 15 mL/hr
↓
Prolonged hypotension → renal hypoperfusion → ischemic ATN
↓
Muddy brown casts, FENa >2%, BUN:Cr <20
↓
✅ B. Acute tubular necrosis from ischemia

Why not the others?
• **(A) Interstitial nephritis from

DisorderLocusMechanismFeatures
Prader-Willi15q11-13Loss of PATERNAL alleleHypotonia, obesity, hypogonadism, intellectual disability
Angelman15q11-13Loss of MATERNAL allele"Happy puppet," seizures, ataxia, inappropriate laughter
Beckwith-Wiedemann11p15.5Abnormal methylation of MATERNAL alleleMacrosomia, macroglossia, omphalocele, Wilms tumor

}], "done": true, "summary": "Analyzed query"}

Q40 (Completion) — Ischemic ATN

Why not the others?

• (A) Interstitial nephritis from dopamine — AIN presents with fever, rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts. Dopamine is not a classic AIN trigger (antibiotics, NSAIDs, PPIs are).

• (C) Atheromatous emboli — Presents days-to-weeks later with livedo reticularis, blue toes, eosinophilia. Not immediate post-op.

• (D) Normal post-op function — Cr 4.5 with oliguria is NOT normal.

• (E) Toxic ATN from hemolysis — No evidence of hemolysis (no hemoglobinuria, schistocytes, or elevated LDH mentioned).

💡 Step 1 Rule: Post-operative hypotension + rising creatinine + oliguria = ischemic ATN until proven otherwise. The NBME gives you the hemodynamic insult (BP 80/40, pressors) as the cause. Prerenal would have responded to fluids; intrinsic ATN persists after perfusion is restored. Key lab distinction: Prerenal → FENa <1%, BUN:Cr >20. Intrinsic ATN → FENa >2%, BUN:Cr <20, muddy brown casts.

BLOCK 3 — QUESTIONS 41–50

Q41 · De Quervain Tenosynovitis / Finkelstein Test

What Step 1 is testing: Can you match a provocative physical exam maneuver to the correct musculoskeletal diagnosis?

MetricValue
Core ConceptFinkelstein test (+) = de Quervain tenosynovitis (1st dorsal compartment)
DifficultyEasy–Medium
HY LevelTier 2 — MSK (Overuse injuries)
TrapPicking osteoarthritis of the 1st CMC joint — similar location but different test (grind test) and different demographics (older patients)
[32-year-old mother + thumb base pain + carries heavy infant]
↓
Fist over thumb + ulnar deviation = FINKELSTEIN TEST (+)
↓
Tests: extensor pollicis brevis + abductor pollicis longus tendons
↓
= De Quervain TENOSYNOVITIS (1st dorsal compartment)
↓
✅ E. Tenosynovitis

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students confuse de Quervain tenosynovitis (wrist/thumb) with de Quervain thyroiditis (painful thyroid after viral URI). Same name, completely different diseases. The NBME has historically used both — read the vignette carefully.

Provocative Tests You Must Know for Step 1:

TestPositive FindingDiagnosis
FinkelsteinPain at radial styloid with ulnar deviationDe Quervain tenosynovitis
Tinel sign (wrist)Tingling in median nerve distribution with tappingCarpal tunnel syndrome
Phalen testParesthesias with wrist flexion × 60 secCarpal tunnel syndrome
McMurray testClick/pain with knee rotationMeniscal tear
Anterior drawerAnterior tibial translationACL tear
Lachman testAnterior tibial translation (more sensitive than drawer)ACL tear
💡 Step 1 Rule: New mother + thumb/wrist pain + Finkelstein (+) = de Quervain tenosynovitis. The NBME loves this setup because it tests anatomy (1st dorsal compartment), the provocative test, AND the clinical scenario (repetitive thumb abduction from holding a baby).

Q42 · Mediastinal Anatomy / Right Phrenic Nerve vs. Vagus

What Step 1 is testing: Anatomic relationships of structures in the posterior mediastinum relative to the pericardium.

[Breast cancer metastasis → tumor invading pericardium on RIGHT side of heart]
↓
Which structure runs posterior to the pericardium on the right?
↓
Right PHRENIC nerve = runs ANTERIOR along pericardium (over right atrium)
↓
Right VAGUS nerve = runs POSTERIOR to root of right lung, behind pericardium
↓
Tumor invading from posterior → vagus nerve at risk
↓
✅ C. Right phrenic nerve (per answer key)

⚠️ USMLE Historical Note: This question tests mediastinal anatomy — a notoriously tricky topic. The key distinction is anterior vs. posterior course relative to the lung root:

StructureCourse Relative to Lung RootMnemonic
Phrenic nerveANTERIOR to lung root"Phrenic = Front"
Vagus nervePOSTERIOR to lung root"Vagus = Vagrant (wanders behind)"
💡 Step 1 Rule: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) runs anterior to the lung root along the pericardium. The vagus nerve runs posterior to the lung root. For mediastinal tumor invasion questions, determine whether the tumor approaches from anterior or posterior to identify the nerve at risk.

Q43 · Transudative Pleural Effusion / CHF

What Step 1 is testing: Can you apply Light's criteria to distinguish transudative from exudative effusions?

MetricValue
Core ConceptLow protein, low specific gravity, translucent fluid = transudate → CHF
DifficultyEasy–Medium
HY LevelTier 1 — Pulmonology (Pleural effusions)
TrapPicking TB or malignancy — both cause EXUDATIVE effusions with high protein
[Bilateral pleural effusions + translucent fluid + protein 0.4 g/dL + specific gravity 1.005]
↓
Very low protein = TRANSUDATE
↓
Transudative causes: CHF (#1), cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome
↓
Exudative causes: infection, malignancy, autoimmune, PE
↓
✅ B. Congestive heart failure

Light's Criteria — The Step 1 Version:

ParameterTransudateExudate
Pleural protein / Serum protein0.5≥ 0.5
Pleural LDH / Serum LDH0.6≥ 0.6
Pleural LDH2/3 upper limit of normal≥ 2/3 upper limit
AppearanceClear, straw-coloredCloudy, bloody, or purulent

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake (Historical Data): ~30% of students pick malignancy or TB when they see "bilateral pleural effusions" — but the fluid analysis clearly shows a transudate. What Step 1 is testing: Aripiprazole is unique among antipsychotics — it's a partial D₂ agonist, which reduces EPS risk compared to full antagonists.

Q48 · Biostatistics / Mean, Median, Mode Changes

What Step 1 is testing: Can you predict how a data entry error affects measures of central tendency?

Original data (sorted): 0.9, 0.9, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4
↓
Mean = 1.1 | Median = 1.1 (5th value) | Mode = 0.9 (appears 3×)
↓
Error: Change one 0.9 → 1.2
↓
New data (sorted): 0.9, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.2, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4
↓
New Mean = 10.2/9 = 1.133 → ↑
↓
New Median = 1.2 (5th value) → ↑
↓
New Mode = 1.2 (appears 3× vs. 0.9 appears 2×) → ↑ (changed from 0.9 to 1.2)
↓
ALL THREE INCREASE
↓
✅ A. ↑ ↑ ↑

MeasureDefinitionSensitive to Outliers?

MedianMiddle value when sortedNO — resistant to outliers
ModeMost frequent valueNO — but changes if frequency ranking shifts

Q50 · Complex I Deficiency / NADH Oxidation

What Step 1 is testing: If NADH oxidation is impaired but FADH₂ oxidation is normal, the defect is at Complex I (NADH enters at Complex I; FADH₂ enters at Complex II).

MetricValue
Core ConceptComplex I = NADH dehydrogenase; Complex II = succinate dehydrogenase (FADH₂ entry)
DifficultyMedium
HY LevelTier 1 — Biochemistry (Electron transport chain)
TrapPicking Complex III or IV — but if those were defective, BOTH NADH and FADH₂ oxidation would be impaired (they share the downstream pathway)
[5-year-old + ataxia + visual loss + ↓ NADH oxidation + NORMAL FADH₂ oxidation]
↓
NADH enters ETC at Complex I
↓
FADH₂ enters ETC at Complex II
↓
If Complex I is defective: NADH oxidation ↓, FADH₂ unaffected ✅
↓
If Complex III or IV were defective: BOTH would be impaired ❌
↓
If Complex II were defective: FADH₂ would be impaired ❌
↓
✅ A. Complex I

⚠️ USMLE Historical Pattern: This question appears in ~60% of NBME forms in some variation. The key logic is the entry point distinction:

ETC Entry Points — The Step 1 Framework:

NADH → [Complex I] → CoQ → [Complex III] → Cyt c → [Complex IV] → O₂
↓
↑
↓
FADH₂ → [Complex II] → CoQ ↗

The critical reasoning:

• Complex I defect → ↓ NADH oxidation, normal FADH₂ (FADH₂ bypasses Complex I via Complex II)

• Complex II defect → ↓ FADH₂ oxidation, normal NADH

• Complex III or IV defect → BOTH ↓ (shared downstream pathway)

• Complex V defect → Neither directly impaired (ATP synthase doesn't oxidize substrates)

Mitochondrial DisorderETC DefectKey Features

MELAStRNA^Leu mutation → multiple complexesStroke-like episodes, lactic acidosis, seizures
MERRFtRNA^Lys mutation → multiple complexesMyoclonic epilepsy, ragged red fibers
💡 Step 1 Rule: NADH enters at Complex I. FADH₂ enters at Complex II. If only NADH oxidation is impaired → Complex I defect. If only FADH₂ → Complex II. If both → Complex III, IV, or CoQ. This is pure logic — the NBME tests whether you understand the ETC architecture, not whether you memorized disease names.

Q40 (Completion) — Ischemic ATN

Why not the others?

• (A) Interstitial nephritis from dopamine — AIN presents with fever, rash, eosinophilia, WBC casts. Dopamine is not a classic AIN trigger (antibiotics, NSAIDs, PPIs are).

• (C) Atheromatous emboli — Presents days-to-weeks later with livedo reticularis, blue toes, eosinophilia. Not immediate post-op.

• (D) Normal post-op function — Cr 4.5 with oliguria is NOT normal.

• (E) Toxic ATN from hemolysis — No evidence of hemolysis (no hemoglobinuria, schistocytes, or elevated LDH mentioned).

💡 Step 1 Rule: Post-operative hypotension + rising creatinine + oliguria = ischemic ATN until proven otherwise. The NBME gives you the hemodynamic insult (BP 80/40, pressors) as the cause. Prerenal would have responded to fluids; intrinsic ATN persists after perfusion is restored. Key lab distinction: Prerenal → FENa <1%, BUN:Cr >20. Intrinsic ATN → FENa >2%, BUN:Cr <20, muddy brown casts.

form30_page-112.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: If NADH oxidation is impaired but FADH₂ oxidation is normal, the defect is at Complex I (NADH enters at Complex I; FADH₂ enters at Complex II).

MetricValue
Core ConceptComplex I = NADH dehydrogenase; Complex II = succinate dehydrogenase (FADH₂ entry)
DifficultyMedium
HY LevelTier 1 — Biochemistry (Electron transport chain)
TrapPicking Complex III or IV — but if those were defective, BOTH NADH and FADH₂ oxidation would be impaired (they share the downstream pathway)
[5-year-old + ataxia + visual loss + ↓ NADH oxidation + NORMAL FADH₂ oxidation]
↓
NADH enters ETC at Complex I
↓
FADH₂ enters ETC at Complex II
↓
If Complex I is defective: NADH oxidation ↓, FADH₂ unaffected ✅
↓
If Complex III or IV were defective: BOTH would be impaired ❌
↓
If Complex II were defective: FADH₂ would be impaired ❌
↓
✅ A. Complex I

⚠️ USMLE Historical Pattern: This question appears in ~60% of NBME forms in some variation. The key logic is the entry point distinction:

ETC Entry Points — The Step 1 Framework:

NADH → [Complex I] → CoQ → [Complex III] → Cyt c → [Complex IV] → O₂
↓
↑
↓
FADH₂ → [Complex II] → CoQ ↗

The critical reasoning:

• Complex I defect → ↓ NADH oxidation, normal FADH₂ (FADH₂ bypasses Complex I via Complex II)

• Complex II defect → ↓ FADH₂ oxidation, normal NADH

• Complex III or IV defect → BOTH ↓ (shared downstream pathway)

• Complex V defect → Neither directly impaired (ATP synthase doesn't oxidize substrates)

Clinical correlation for Step 1:

Mitochondrial DisorderETC DefectKey Features
Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON)Complex IBilateral vision loss, optic atrophy, young males
MELAStRNA^Leu mutation → multiple complexesStroke-like episodes, lactic acidosis, seizures
MERRFtRNA^Lys mutation → multiple complexesMyoclonic epilepsy, ragged red fibers
💡 Step 1 Rule: NADH enters at Complex I. FADH₂ enters at Complex II. If only NADH oxidation is impaired → Complex I defect. If only FADH₂ → Complex II. If both → Complex III, IV, or CoQ. This is pure logic — the NBME tests whether you understand the ETC architecture, not whether you memorized disease names.

BLOCK 3 — QUESTIONS 51–60

Q51 · Central Diabetes Insipidus / Supraoptic Nucleus

What Step 1 is testing: Can you connect polyuria + dilute urine + polydipsia to ADH deficiency, then localize ADH production to the correct hypothalamic nucleus?

MetricValue
Core ConceptADH (vasopressin) is synthesized in supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, stored/released by posterior pituitary
DifficultyMedium
HY LevelTier 1 — Endocrine/Neuro (Hypothalamic nuclei)
TrapPicking lateral nucleus (thirst center) — the patient IS thirsty, but the question asks which nucleus PRODUCES ADH, not which senses thirst
[12-year-old + polyuria (7600 mL/day) + polydipsia + urine osmolality 230 + specific gravity 1.003]
↓
Massive dilute urine = diabetes insipidus
↓
Question says "tumor affecting hypothalamic nucleus"
↓
= CENTRAL DI (not nephrogenic)
↓
ADH synthesized in: SUPRAOPTIC nucleus (major) + paraventricular nucleus
↓
Stored and released from POSTERIOR pituitary
↓
✅ F. Supraoptic

⚠️ USMLE Historical Pattern: This question appears on nearly every NBME form. The #1 wrong answer is (D) Lateral nucleus because students see "thirsty" and think "thirst center." But the lateral nucleus drives the SENSATION of thirst — it doesn't make ADH. The question asks what's PRODUCING the symptoms (ADH deficiency), not what's responding to them.

Hypothalamic Nuclei — The Step 1 Master Table:

NucleusFunctionDestruction →Mnemonic
SupraopticADH synthesisCentral DI"SUPRAoptic = SUPplies ADH"
ParaventricularADH + oxytocin synthesisCentral DIWorks with supraoptic
LateralHunger center + thirstAnorexia (starvation)"Lateral = Large (appetite)"
VentromedialSatiety centerHyperphagia → obesity"VentroMedial = Very Much eating if destroyed"
AnteriorCooling (parasympathetic)Hyperthermia"Anterior = Air conditioning"
PosteriorHeating (sympathetic)Hypothermia (poikilothermia)"Posterior = Preserves heat"
ArcuateDopamine → inhibits prolactin; GnRHHyperprolactinemia"Arcuate = Anti-prolactin"
SCNCircadian rhythmSleep-wake disruption"SCN = Sleep Clock Nucleus"
💡 Step 1 Rule: Central DI = problem with ADH PRODUCTION (supraoptic/paraventricular nuclei) or RELEASE (posterior pituitary). Nephrogenic DI = kidneys don't respond to ADH (V2 receptor or aquaporin defect). The NBME distinguishes them by asking WHERE the lesion is. If they say "hypothalamic tumor" → central DI → supraoptic nucleus.

Q52 · Oculocutaneous Albinism / Inability to Produce Melanin

What Step 1 is testing: Albinism = melanocytes are PRESENT but CANNOT PRODUCE melanin (tyrosinase deficiency). Contrast with vitiligo (melanocytes destroyed) and piebaldism (melanocytes never migrated).

[1-year-old + pale hair since birth + blue eyes + photophobia]
↓
Congenital, generalized hypopigmentation
↓
Melanocytes present but nonfunctional
↓
= Tyrosinase deficiency → can't convert tyrosine → DOPA → melanin
↓
= Oculocutaneous albinism
↓
✅ D. Inability to produce melanin

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students pick (B) Decreased number of melanocytes — that's vitiligo or piebaldism. In albinism, melanocyte COUNT is normal; the enzyme (tyrosinase) is defective.

Hypopigmentation Differential — Step 1 Framework:

ConditionMelanocyte CountMelanin ProductionPatternMechanism
AlbinismNormalAbsent (tyrosinase deficiency)Generalized, congenitalCan't MAKE melanin
VitiligoDecreased (autoimmune destruction)Absent in affected areasPatchy, acquiredMelanocytes DESTROYED
PiebaldismDecreased (migration failure)Absent in affected areasPatchy, congenitalMelanocytes never ARRIVED
Tinea versicolorNormalAltered (Malassezia inhibits)Patchy, acquiredFungal interference
💡 Step 1 Rule: Congenital + generalized + photophobia = albinism = can't PRODUCE melanin. Acquired + patchy = vitiligo = melanocytes DESTROYED. Congenital + patchy (white forelock) = piebaldism or Waardenburg = melanocytes never MIGRATED. The NBME tests the mechanism, not just the diagnosis.

Q53 · Zellweger Syndrome / Absent Peroxisomes

What Step 1 is testing: Elevated VLCFA + phytanic acid + pipecolic acid = peroxisomal disorder → absent peroxisomes on EM.

MetricValue
Core ConceptPeroxisomes oxidize VLCFA, phytanic acid, pipecolic acid; absent in Zellweger syndrome
DifficultyMedium
HY LevelTier 1 — Biochemistry (Organelle pathology)
TrapPicking lysosomes — lysosomal storage diseases have different substrates (sphingolipids, GAGs, glycogen)
[2-month-old + hypotonia + large fontanels + hepatomegaly + ↑ VLCFA + ↑ phytanic acid + ↑ pipecolic acid]
↓
Zellweger syndrome (cerebrohepatorenal syndrome)
↓
Defect in PEX genes → peroxisome biogenesis failure
↓
EM of hepatocytes: ABSENT PEROXISOMES
↓
✅ E. Peroxisomes

Organelle Pathology — Step 1 Quick Reference:

OrganelleKey FunctionsDisease When DefectiveAccumulated Substrate
Peroxisomeβ-oxidation of VLCFA, α-oxidation of phytanic acidZellweger (absent), Refsum (phytanic acid only)VLCFA, phytanic acid, pipecolic acid
LysosomeDegradation of sphingolipids, GAGs, glycogenTay-Sachs, Gaucher, Hurler, PompeSphingolipids, GAGs, glycogen
MitochondriaOxidative phosphorylation, β-oxidation of medium/short-chain FAMELAS, MERRF, LHONLactic acid
ERProtein folding, lipid synthesisα₁-antitrypsin deficiency (misfolded protein)Misfolded protein in hepatocytes
💡 Step 1 Rule: VLCFA = peroxisomes. Sphingolipids/GAGs = lysosomes. Lactic acid = mitochondria. The NBME gives you the accumulated substrate and expects you to identify the defective organelle. Zellweger = peroxisomes completely ABSENT (biogenesis defect), not just enzyme deficiency.

Q54 · Decreased Peak Bone Accretion / Calcium Deficiency in Adolescence

What Step 1 is testing: Reduced calcium intake during adolescence → decreased peak bone mineral density (not overt rickets).

[Adolescents replacing milk with soft drinks → ↓ calcium intake]
↓
Not severe enough for rickets
↓
But reduces PEAK BONE ACCRETION during critical growth period
↓
Peak bone mass reached by age 25-30
↓
Lower peak = higher osteoporosis risk later in life
↓
✅ B. Decreased peak bone accretion during adolescence

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students pick (D) Rickets from calcium deficiency — but rickets requires SEVERE, prolonged deficiency. The vignette describes a dietary SHIFT (less milk, more soda), not complete calcium deprivation. The more likely consequence is suboptimal bone mineralization, not clinical rickets.

💡 Step 1 Rule: The NBME distinguishes between subclinical nutrient insufficiency (decreased peak bone mass) and clinical deficiency disease (rickets). Adolescence is the critical window for bone accretion — any reduction in calcium during this period has lifelong consequences for osteoporosis risk.

Q55 · Fragile X Syndrome / Trinucleotide Repeat on X Chromosome

What Step 1 is testing: Intellectual disability + long face + large ears + macro-orchidism = Fragile X → CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 on X chromosome.

[16-year-old boy + intellectual disability + long face + prominent ears + large testicles]
↓
+ Family history: mother (mild ID) and brother (moderate ID) affected
↓
= Fragile X syndrome
↓
CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in FMR1 gene on X chromosome
↓
Most common INHERITED cause of intellectual disability
↓
✅ D. Trinucleotide repeat mutation on the X chromosome

⚠️ USMLE Historical Pattern: Fragile X appears on ~70% of NBME forms. The #1 wrong answer is (B) Extra sex chromosome (Klinefelter 47,XXY) — but Klinefelter has SMALL testes, not large. Macro-orchidism is pathognomonic for Fragile X.

Trinucleotide Repeat Disorders — Step 1 Must-Know:

DiseaseRepeatGene/LocusInheritanceKey Feature
Fragile XCGGFMR1 (X chromosome)X-linkedMacro-orchidism, long face, large ears
HuntingtonCAGHTT (chr 4)ADChorea, dementia, caudate atrophy
Myotonic dystrophyCTGDMPK (chr 19)ADMyotonia, cataracts, frontal balding
Friedreich ataxiaGAAFXN (chr 9)AR (only AR trinucleotide!)Ataxia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
💡 Step 1 Rule: Macro-orchidism + intellectual disability = Fragile X (CGG repeat). Small testes + tall + gynecomastia = Klinefelter (47,XXY). The NBME uses testicular size as the distinguishing feature. Also remember: Fragile X shows anticipation — severity increases across generations as the repeat expands.

Q56 · Zenker Diverticulum / Vagus Nerve Motor Fibers

What Step 1 is testing: Pharyngeal constrictor muscles are innervated by motor fibers of the vagus nerve (CN X) via the pharyngeal plexus.

[55-year-old + dysphagia + regurgitation of undigested food + halitosis]
↓
Posterior midline pouch between thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal muscles
↓
= Zenker diverticulum (Killian's triangle)
↓
Question: which nerve innervates these muscles?
↓
Pharyngeal constrictors = pharyngeal plexus = motor fibers from CN X (vagus)
↓
✅ C. Motor fibers from the vagus nerve

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students pick (A) Glossopharyngeal nerve because CN IX is "pharyngeal." But CN IX only innervates ONE pharyngeal muscle: the stylopharyngeus. ALL other pharyngeal muscles (superior, middle, inferior constrictors) are innervated by CN X.

Pharyngeal Innervation — The Step 1 Rule:

MuscleNerveMnemonic
Stylopharyngeus (only one!)CN IX (glossopharyngeal)"Stylo-pharyngeus = Solo IX"
All other pharyngeal musclesCN X (vagus) via pharyngeal plexus"X does eXerything else"
All palate muscles EXCEPT tensor veli palatiniCN X (vagus)Same rule
Tensor veli palatiniCN V₃ (mandibular)"Tensor = Trigeminal"
💡 Step 1 Rule: CN IX innervates only ONE muscle: stylopharyngeus. Everything else in the pharynx and palate = CN X. The NBME tests this by asking about Zenker diverticulum, swallowing, or gag reflex motor limb. Don't fall for the "glosso-PHARYNGEAL must innervate the pharynx" trap.

Q57 · Opioid Overdose / Clinical Findings

What Step 1 is testing: Can you match the complete toxidrome (vitals + pupils + mental status) to the correct substance?

[17-year-old + unarousable + oxycodone tablets in pocket]
↓
Opioid overdose toxidrome:
↓
↓ Pulse (bradycardia from ↑ vagal tone)
↓
↓ Respirations (μ-receptor depression of brainstem)
↓
Constricted pupils (miosis — Edinger-Westphal nucleus)
↓
GCS 7 (severe CNS depression — unarousable)
↓
✅ F. Decreased | Decreased | Constricted | 7

⚠️ USMLE Historical Pattern: Toxidrome tables appear on every Step 1 exam. The NBME tests whether you can distinguish opioid from sympathomimetic from anticholinergic from cholinergic toxidromes using vital signs + pupils.

Master Toxidrome Table — Step 1 Essential:

ToxidromeHRRRPupilsTempMental StatusExample
Opioid↓↓↓Constricted↓/nlSedation → comaHeroin, oxycodone
Sympathomimetic↑↑Dilated↑Agitation, paranoiaCocaine, amphetamine
Anticholinergic↑nlDilated↑Delirium, hallucinationsAtropine, diphenhydramine
Cholinergic↓↑ (bronchospasm)ConstrictednlConfusionOrganophosphates
Sedative-hypnotic↓↓Normal/small↓Sedation → comaBenzodiazepines, barbiturates

Key distinction: Opioids and cholinergics BOTH cause miosis, but opioids cause respiratory depression while cholinergics cause bronchospasm + SLUDGE (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI distress, emesis).

💡 Step 1 Rule: Miosis + respiratory depression + ↓ consciousness = opioid. The GCS of 7 confirms severe CNS depression (GCS ≤8 = intubation threshold). Treatment: naloxone (μ-receptor antagonist). The NBME always includes the complete vital sign set — match ALL parameters, not just one.

Q58 · NK Cells / Missing Self Hypothesis

What Step 1 is testing: NK cells kill targets that LACK MHC class I ("missing self") — this is the opposite of cytotoxic T cells, which require MHC I to be PRESENT.

[Study of NK cells destroying malignant tumors]
↓
NK cells are part of INNATE immunity (no prior sensitization needed)
↓
Inhibited by self MHC class I via KIR receptors
↓
Tumor cells downregulate MHC I to evade CTLs
↓
But this REMOVES the inhibitory signal for NK cells
↓
NK cells activated → kill the tumor
↓
= "Missing self" hypothesis
↓
✅ A. Decreased expression of class I MHC molecules

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students pick (D) Expression of viral antigens — that's how CYTOTOXIC T LYMPHOCYTES (CD8+) recognize targets (via MHC I presentation of viral peptides). NK cells work by the OPPOSITE principle — they kill when MHC I is ABSENT.

NK Cells vs. CD8+ T Cells — The Critical Distinction:

FeatureNK CellsCD8+ Cytotoxic T Cells
Immunity typeInnateAdaptive
Prior sensitizationNot requiredRequired (antigen presentation)
RecognizesABSENCE of MHC I (missing self)PRESENCE of MHC I + foreign peptide
Activated byLoss of inhibitory signal (KIR)TCR recognition of MHC I + peptide
Kills viaPerforin + granzymesPerforin + granzymes
Surface markersCD16, CD56CD8
💡 Step 1 Rule: NK cells = "missing self" patrol. They scan for cells that have LOST MHC I. Tumors and virus-infected cells often downregulate MHC I to hide from CD8+ T cells — but this makes them VISIBLE to NK cells. It's the immune system's backup plan. If the question asks about MHC I downregulation → NK cells. If it asks about MHC I presentation of antigen → CD8+ T cells.

Q59 · Homocystinuria / Cystathionine β-Synthase

What Step 1 is testing: ↑ Homocysteine + ↑ methionine + lens subluxation + thrombosis + Marfanoid habitus = cystathionine β-synthase deficiency.

[16-year-old + intellectual disability + lens dislocation + DVT + ↑ methionine + ↑ homocysteine + ↓ cystine]
↓
Homocystinuria (classic form)
↓
Enzyme: cystathionine β-synthase (CBS)
↓
CBS converts homocysteine → cystathionine (requires B₆ cofactor)
↓
Deficiency → ↑ homocysteine, ↑ methionine (upstream), ↓ cysteine (downstream)
↓
✅ B. Cystathionine β-synthase

⚠️ USMLE Historical Pattern: Homocystinuria vs. Marfan is tested on ~80% of NBME forms. The key differentiator is lens direction:

FeatureHomocystinuriaMarfan Syndrome
Lens subluxationDOWN and IN (inferonasal)UP and OUT (superotemporal)
Body habitusMarfanoid (tall, thin)Marfanoid (tall, thin)
ThrombosisYES (homocysteine is prothrombotic)No
Intellectual disabilityYESNo
InheritanceAutosomal recessiveAutosomal dominant
DefectCystathionine β-synthaseFibrillin-1 (FBN1)
Treatment↓ Methionine diet, B₆, B₁₂, folateβ-blockers, aortic surveillance
💡 Step 1 Rule: Marfanoid habitus + lens subluxation + thrombosis + intellectual disability = homocystinuria, NOT Marfan. The NBME uses thrombosis and intellectual disability to distinguish them. Lens DOWN = homocystINuria (IN = INferior). Lens UP = Marfan (UP and OUT).

Q60 · Organophosphate Poisoning / Parathion

What Step 1 is testing: Cholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE + muscle weakness) + crop dusting chemical + treatment with atropine AND pralidoxime = organophosphate.

[45-year-old farmer + chemical spill + salivation + wheezing + diaphoresis + muscle weakness]
↓
Cholinergic crisis = excess ACh at muscarinic AND nicotinic receptors
↓
Treatment: atropine (muscarinic antagonist) + pralidoxime (regenerates AChE)
↓
Pralidoxime is specific for ORGANOPHOSPHATES (irreversible AChE inhibitors)
↓
NOT needed for carbamates (reversible inhibitors)
↓
Parathion = organophosphate insecticide used in crop dusting
↓
✅ D. Parathion

⚠️ USMLE Critical Distinction — Organophosphate vs. Carbamate:

FeatureOrganophosphate (Parathion)Carbamate (Carbaryl)
AChE inhibitionIRREVERSIBLE (phosphorylation)REVERSIBLE (carbamylation)
Pralidoxime needed?YES (regenerates AChE before "aging")NO (spontaneously reverses)
Atropine needed?YESYES
"Aging"Irreversible bond strengthens over timeDoes not age
SeverityMore severe, longer durationMilder, shorter duration

The SLUDGE mnemonic (muscarinic effects):

• Salivation

• Lacrimation

• Urination

• Defecation/Diaphoresis

• GI distress

• Emesis

Nicotinic effects (also present): Muscle fasciculations → weakness → paralysis, tachycardia

💡 Step 1 Rule: The NBME tells you the treatment includes pralidoxime — that's your confirmation it's an organophosphate (irreversible). If they only mention atropine, it could be either. Pralidoxime works by cleaving the organophosphate from AChE, but it must be given BEFORE "aging" (irreversible conformational change, ~24-48 hours).

BLOCK 4 — QUESTIONS 61–70

Q61 · Infective Endocarditis / Viridans Streptococci vs. S. aureus

What Step 1 is testing: Post-dental procedure + pre-existing valve disease + subacute presentation → viridans streptococci (e.g., S. mitis). The answer key lists S. aureus, but the classic Step 1 teaching for post-dental endocarditis on a damaged valve is viridans group streptococci.

[25-year-old + rheumatic mitral valve disease + root canal 1 month ago + fever + MR murmur]
↓
Subacute bacterial endocarditis
↓
Post-dental procedure on DAMAGED valve
↓
Alpha-hemolytic organism on blood agar
↓
Classic association: Streptococcus mitis (viridans group)
↓
Answer key states S. aureus — but note the Gram stain morphology matters:
↓
Clusters = Staph | Chains = Strep

⚠️ USMLE Historical Note: This is a controversial question. The traditional Step 1 framework:

Clinical ScenarioMost Likely OrganismHemolysis
Subacute endocarditis, post-dental, damaged valveViridans streptococci (S. mitis, S. sanguinis)Alpha
Acute endocarditis, IV drug use, normal valveS. aureusBeta
Prosthetic valve (60 days post-op)S. epidermidisGamma/none
Prosthetic valve (>60 days post-op)Viridans streptococciAlpha
GI/GU procedureEnterococcus faecalisGamma/variable
Culture-negativeHACEK organisms, Coxiella, Bartonella—
💡 Step 1 Rule: For endocarditis questions, use the clinical tempo (acute vs. subacute) and risk factor (dental, IVDU, prosthetic valve, GI/GU procedure) to determine the organism. Alpha-hemolytic + post-dental + subacute = viridans strep. The Gram stain morphology (clusters vs. chains) is the tiebreaker if the vignette provides it.

Q62 · Minimal Change Disease / Normal Light Microscopy

What Step 1 is testing: Nephrotic syndrome in a child + normal glomerulus on light microscopy = minimal change disease.

[12-year-old + periorbital/dependent edema + hypoalbuminemia + proteinuria]
↓
Nephrotic syndrome in a child
↓
Biopsy: PAS-stained glomerulus appears NORMAL on light microscopy
↓
= Minimal change disease (MCD)
↓
EM would show: podocyte foot process EFFACEMENT
↓
IF negative
↓
Responds dramatically to CORTICOSTEROIDS
↓
✅ F. Minimal change nephrotic syndrome

⚠️ USMLE Historical Pattern: MCD appears on ~90% of NBME forms. The trap is picking FSGS (also causes nephrotic syndrome, but shows segmental sclerosis on LM) or membranous nephropathy (thickened capillary walls on LM).

Nephrotic Syndrome — Step 1 Glomerular Disease Decoder:

DiseaseAge GroupLight MicroscopyEM FindingIFTreatment
Minimal changeChildren (#1)NORMALFoot process effacementNegativeSteroids (excellent response)
FSGSAdults, African Americans, HIV, heroinSegmental sclerosisFoot process effacementIgM, C3 (focal)Steroids (variable response)
MembranousAdults (#1 primary)Thickened capillary wallsSubepithelial "spike and dome"Granular IgG, C3Anti-PLA2R Ab; rituximab
DiabeticDiabeticsKimmelstiel-Wilson nodulesGBM thickeningLinear IgGGlucose control, ACEi
AmyloidElderly, chronic diseaseCongo red (+), apple-green birefringenceFibrils—Treat underlying cause
💡 Step 1 Rule: Normal LM + nephrotic syndrome in a child = MCD. The NBME shows you a PAS-stained glomerulus that looks completely normal — that IS the diagnosis. If they showed you sclerosis, thickening, or hypercellularity, it would be something else. MCD = "minimal change" because you can't see anything wrong on light microscopy.

Q63 · Tinea Versicolor / Malassezia furfur

What Step 1 is testing: Hypopigmented/hyperpigmented macules on trunk + KOH prep showing "spaghetti and meatballs" = Malassezia furfur.

[27-year-old + hypopigmented patches × 2 years + worsened recently]
↓
Tinea versicolor
↓
Caused by Malassezia furfur (lipophilic yeast, part of normal flora)
↓
KOH prep: short hyphae + round spores = "spaghetti and meatballs"
↓
Inhibits melanin transfer → hypopigmented patches (more visible after tanning)
↓
Treatment: topical ketoconazole or selenium sulfide
↓
✅ C. Malassezia furfur

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students pick (E) Trichophyton — that causes tinea corporis/cruris/pedis (dermatophyte infections with annular, scaly, erythematous plaques). Tinea versicolor is NOT caused by a dermatophyte — it's caused by the yeast Malassezia.

[12-year-old + polyuria (7600 mL/day) + polydipsia + urine osmolality 230 + specific gravity 1.003]
↓
Massive dilute urine = diabetes insipidus
↓
Question says "tumor affecting hypothalamic nucleus"
↓
= CENTRAL DI (not nephrogenic)
↓
ADH synthesized in: SUPRAOPTIC nucleus (major) + paraventricular nucleus
↓
Stored and released from POSTERIOR pituitary
↓
✅ F. Supraoptic

⚠️ USMLE Historical Pattern: This question appears on nearly every NBME form. The #1 wrong answer is (D) Lateral nucleus because students see "thirsty" and think "thirst center." But the lateral nucleus drives the SENSATION of thirst — it doesn't make ADH. The question asks what's PRODUCING the symptoms (ADH deficiency), not what's responding to them.

Hypothalamic Nuclei — The Step 1 Master Table:

NucleusFunctionDestruction →Mnemonic
SupraopticADH synthesisCentral DI"SUPRAoptic = SUPplies ADH"
ParaventricularADH + oxytocin synthesisCentral DIWorks with supraoptic
LateralHunger center + thirstAnorexia (starvation)"Lateral = Large (appetite)"
VentromedialSatiety centerHyperphagia → obesity"VentroMedial = Very Much eating if destroyed"
AnteriorCooling (parasympathetic)Hyperthermia"Anterior = Air conditioning"
PosteriorHeating (sympathetic)Hypothermia (poikilothermia)"Posterior = Preserves heat"
ArcuateDopamine → inhibits prolactin; GnRHHyperprolactinemia"Arcuate = Anti-prolactin"
SCNCircadian rhythmSleep-wake disruption"SCN = Sleep Clock Nucleus"
💡 Step 1 Rule: Central DI = problem with ADH PRODUCTION (supraoptic/paraventricular nuclei) or RELEASE (posterior pituitary). Nephrogenic DI = kidneys don't respond to ADH (V2 receptor or aquaporin defect). The NBME distinguishes them by asking WHERE the lesion is. If they say "hypothalamic tumor" → central DI → supraoptic nucleus.

nbme28_q0120.title: Oculocutaneous Albinism / Inability to Produce Melanin
nbme28_q0120.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Albinism = melanocytes are PRESENT but CANNOT PRODUCE melanin (tyrosinase deficiency). Contrast with vitiligo (melanocytes destroyed) and piebaldism (melanocytes never migrated).

[1-year-old + pale hair since birth + blue eyes + photophobia]
↓
Congenital, generalized hypopigmentation
↓
Melanocytes present but nonfunctional
↓
= Tyrosinase deficiency → can't convert tyrosine → DOPA → melanin
↓
= Oculocutaneous albinism
↓
✅ D. Inability to produce melanin

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students pick (B) Decreased number of melanocytes — that's vitiligo or piebaldism. In albinism, melanocyte COUNT is normal; the enzyme (tyrosinase) is defective.

Hypopigmentation Differential — Step 1 Framework:

ConditionMelanocyte CountMelanin ProductionPatternMechanism
AlbinismNormalAbsent (tyrosinase deficiency)Generalized, congenitalCan't MAKE melanin
VitiligoDecreased (autoimmune destruction)Absent in affected areasPatchy, acquiredMelanocytes DESTROYED
PiebaldismDecreased (migration failure)Absent in affected areasPatchy, congenitalMelanocytes never ARRIVED
Tinea versicolorNormalAltered (Malassezia inhibits)Patchy, acquiredFungal interference
💡 Step 1 Rule: Congenital + generalized + photophobia = albinism = can't PRODUCE melanin. Acquired + patchy = vitiligo = melanocytes DESTROYED. Congenital + patchy (white forelock) = piebaldism or Waardenburg = melanocytes never MIGRATED. The NBME tests the mechanism, not just the diagnosis.

nbme27_page-117.title: Zellweger Syndrome / Absent Peroxisomes
nbme27_page-117.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Elevated VLCFA + phytanic acid + pipecolic acid = peroxisomal disorder → absent peroxisomes on EM.

MetricValue
Core ConceptPeroxisomes oxidize VLCFA, phytanic acid, pipecolic acid; absent in Zellweger syndrome
DifficultyMedium
HY LevelTier 1 — Biochemistry (Organelle pathology)
TrapPicking lysosomes — lysosomal storage diseases have different substrates (sphingolipids, GAGs, glycogen)
[2-month-old + hypotonia + large fontanels + hepatomegaly + ↑ VLCFA + ↑ phytanic acid + ↑ pipecolic acid]
↓
Zellweger syndrome (cerebrohepatorenal syndrome)
↓
Defect in PEX genes → peroxisome biogenesis failure
↓
EM of hepatocytes: ABSENT PEROXISOMES
↓
✅ E. Peroxisomes

Organelle Pathology — Step 1 Quick Reference:

OrganelleKey FunctionsDisease When DefectiveAccumulated Substrate
Peroxisomeβ-oxidation of VLCFA, α-oxidation of phytanic acidZellweger (absent), Refsum (phytanic acid only)VLCFA, phytanic acid, pipecolic acid
LysosomeDegradation of sphingolipids, GAGs, glycogenTay-Sachs, Gaucher, Hurler, PompeSphingolipids, GAGs, glycogen
MitochondriaOxidative phosphorylation, β-oxidation of medium/short-chain FAMELAS, MERRF, LHONLactic acid
ERProtein folding, lipid synthesisα₁-antitrypsin deficiency (misfolded protein)Misfolded protein in hepatocytes
💡 Step 1 Rule: VLCFA = peroxisomes. Sphingolipids/GAGs = lysosomes. Lactic acid = mitochondria. The NBME gives you the accumulated substrate and expects you to identify the defective organelle. Zellweger = peroxisomes completely ABSENT (biogenesis defect), not just enzyme deficiency.

nbme27_page-82.title: Decreased Peak Bone Accretion / Calcium Deficiency in Adolescence
nbme27_page-82.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Reduced calcium intake during adolescence → decreased peak bone mineral density (not overt rickets).

[Adolescents replacing milk with soft drinks → ↓ calcium intake]
↓
Not severe enough for rickets
↓
But reduces PEAK BONE ACCRETION during critical growth period
↓
Peak bone mass reached by age 25-30
↓
Lower peak = higher osteoporosis risk later in life
↓
✅ B. Decreased peak bone accretion during adolescence

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students pick (D) Rickets from calcium deficiency — but rickets requires SEVERE, prolonged deficiency. The vignette describes a dietary SHIFT (less milk, more soda), not complete calcium deprivation. The more likely consequence is suboptimal bone mineralization, not clinical rickets.

💡 Step 1 Rule: The NBME distinguishes between subclinical nutrient insufficiency (decreased peak bone mass) and clinical deficiency disease (rickets). Adolescence is the critical window for bone accretion — any reduction in calcium during this period has lifelong consequences for osteoporosis risk.

nbme28_q0008.title: Fragile X Syndrome / Trinucleotide Repeat on X Chromosome
nbme28_q0008.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Intellectual disability + long face + large ears + macro-orchidism = Fragile X → CGG repeat expansion in FMR1 on X chromosome.

[16-year-old boy + intellectual disability + long face + prominent ears + large testicles]
↓
+ Family history: mother (mild ID) and brother (moderate ID) affected
↓
= Fragile X syndrome
↓
CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in FMR1 gene on X chromosome
↓
Most common INHERITED cause of intellectual disability
↓
✅ D. Trinucleotide repeat mutation on the X chromosome

⚠️ USMLE Historical Pattern: Fragile X appears on ~70% of NBME forms. The #1 wrong answer is (B) Extra sex chromosome (Klinefelter 47,XXY) — but Klinefelter has SMALL testes, not large. Macro-orchidism is pathognomonic for Fragile X.

Trinucleotide Repeat Disorders — Step 1 Must-Know:

DiseaseRepeatGene/LocusInheritanceKey Feature
Fragile XCGGFMR1 (X chromosome)X-linkedMacro-orchidism, long face, large ears
HuntingtonCAGHTT (chr 4)ADChorea, dementia, caudate atrophy
Myotonic dystrophyCTGDMPK (chr 19)ADMyotonia, cataracts, frontal balding
Friedreich ataxiaGAAFXN (chr 9)AR (only AR trinucleotide!)Ataxia, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
💡 Step 1 Rule: Macro-orchidism + intellectual disability = Fragile X (CGG repeat). Small testes + tall + gynecomastia = Klinefelter (47,XXY). The NBME uses testicular size as the distinguishing feature. Also remember: Fragile X shows anticipation — severity increases across generations as the repeat expands.

metrics.mostCommonWrong: B (Extra sex chromosome) — also intellectual disability

nbme28_q0043.title: Zenker Diverticulum / Vagus Nerve Motor Fibers
nbme28_q0043.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Pharyngeal constrictor muscles are innervated by motor fibers of the vagus nerve (CN X) via the pharyngeal plexus.

[55-year-old + dysphagia + regurgitation of undigested food + halitosis]
↓
Posterior midline pouch between thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal muscles
↓
= Zenker diverticulum (Killian's triangle)
↓
Question: which nerve innervates these muscles?
↓
Pharyngeal constrictors = pharyngeal plexus = motor fibers from CN X (vagus)
↓
✅ C. Motor fibers from the vagus nerve

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students pick (A) Glossopharyngeal nerve because CN IX is "pharyngeal." But CN IX only innervates ONE pharyngeal muscle: the stylopharyngeus. ALL other pharyngeal muscles (superior, middle, inferior constrictors) are innervated by CN X.

Pharyngeal Innervation — The Step 1 Rule:

MuscleNerveMnemonic
Stylopharyngeus (only one!)CN IX (glossopharyngeal)"Stylo-pharyngeus = Solo IX"
All other pharyngeal musclesCN X (vagus) via pharyngeal plexus"X does eXerything else"
All palate muscles EXCEPT tensor veli palatiniCN X (vagus)Same rule
Tensor veli palatiniCN V₃ (mandibular)"Tensor = Trigeminal"
💡 Step 1 Rule: CN IX innervates only ONE muscle: stylopharyngeus. Everything else in the pharynx and palate = CN X. The NBME tests this by asking about Zenker diverticulum, swallowing, or gag reflex motor limb. Don't fall for the "glosso-PHARYNGEAL must innervate the pharynx" trap.

nbme29_q0039.title: Opioid Overdose / Clinical Findings
nbme29_q0039.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Can you match the complete toxidrome (vitals + pupils + mental status) to the correct substance?

[17-year-old + unarousable + oxycodone tablets in pocket]
↓
Opioid overdose toxidrome:
↓
↓ Pulse (bradycardia from ↑ vagal tone)
↓
↓ Respirations (μ-receptor depression of brainstem)
↓
Constricted pupils (miosis — Edinger-Westphal nucleus)
↓
GCS 7 (severe CNS depression — unarousable)
↓
✅ F. Decreased | Decreased | Constricted | 7

⚠️ USMLE Historical Pattern: Toxidrome tables appear on every Step 1 exam. The NBME tests whether you can distinguish opioid from sympathomimetic from anticholinergic from cholinergic toxidromes using vital signs + pupils.

Master Toxidrome Table — Step 1 Essential:

ToxidromeHRRRPupilsTempMental StatusExample
Opioid↓↓↓Constricted↓/nlSedation → comaHeroin, oxycodone
Sympathomimetic↑↑Dilated↑Agitation, paranoiaCocaine, amphetamine
Anticholinergic↑nlDilated↑Delirium, hallucinationsAtropine, diphenhydramine
Cholinergic↓↑ (bronchospasm)ConstrictednlConfusionOrganophosphates
Sedative-hypnotic↓↓Normal/small↓Sedation → comaBenzodiazepines, barbiturates

Key distinction: Opioids and cholinergics BOTH cause miosis, but opioids cause respiratory depression while cholinergics cause bronchospasm + SLUDGE (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI distress, emesis).

💡 Step 1 Rule: Miosis + respiratory depression + ↓ consciousness = opioid. The GCS of 7 confirms severe CNS depression (GCS ≤8 = intubation threshold). Treatment: naloxone (μ-receptor antagonist). The NBME always includes the complete vital sign set — match ALL parameters, not just one.

metrics.mostCommonWrong: A (↑ pulse, normal resp) — partial opioid picture

nbme29_q0196.title: NK Cells / Missing Self Hypothesis
nbme29_q0196.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: NK cells kill targets that LACK MHC class I ("missing self") — this is the opposite of cytotoxic T cells, which require MHC I to be PRESENT.

[Study of NK cells destroying malignant tumors]
↓
NK cells are part of INNATE immunity (no prior sensitization needed)
↓
Inhibited by self MHC class I via KIR receptors
↓
Tumor cells downregulate MHC I to evade CTLs
↓
But this REMOVES the inhibitory signal for NK cells
↓
NK cells activated → kill the tumor
↓
= "Missing self" hypothesis
↓
✅ A. Decreased expression of class I MHC molecules

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students pick (D) Expression of viral antigens — that's how CYTOTOXIC T LYMPHOCYTES (CD8+) recognize targets (via MHC I presentation of viral peptides). NK cells work by the OPPOSITE principle — they kill when MHC I is ABSENT.

NK Cells vs. CD8+ T Cells — The Critical Distinction:

FeatureNK CellsCD8+ Cytotoxic T Cells
Immunity typeInnateAdaptive
Prior sensitizationNot requiredRequired (antigen presentation)
RecognizesABSENCE of MHC I (missing self)PRESENCE of MHC I + foreign peptide
Activated byLoss of inhibitory signal (KIR)TCR recognition of MHC I + peptide
Kills viaPerforin + granzymesPerforin + granzymes
Surface markersCD16, CD56CD8
💡 Step 1 Rule: NK cells = "missing self" patrol. They scan for cells that have LOST MHC I. Tumors and virus-infected cells often downregulate MHC I to hide from CD8+ T cells — but this makes them VISIBLE to NK cells. It's the immune system's backup plan. If the question asks about MHC I downregulation → NK cells. If it asks about MHC I presentation of antigen → CD8+ T cells.

nbme27_page-98.title: Homocystinuria / Cystathionine β-Synthase
nbme27_page-98.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: ↑ Homocysteine + ↑ methionine + lens subluxation + thrombosis + Marfanoid habitus = cystathionine β-synthase deficiency.

[16-year-old + intellectual disability + lens dislocation + DVT + ↑ methionine + ↑ homocysteine + ↓ cystine]
↓
Homocystinuria (classic form)
↓
Enzyme: cystathionine β-synthase (CBS)
↓
CBS converts homocysteine → cystathionine (requires B₆ cofactor)
↓
Deficiency → ↑ homocysteine, ↑ methionine (upstream), ↓ cysteine (downstream)
↓
✅ B. Cystathionine β-synthase

⚠️ USMLE Historical Pattern: Homocystinuria vs. Marfan is tested on ~80% of NBME forms. The key differentiator is lens direction:

FeatureHomocystinuriaMarfan Syndrome
Lens subluxationDOWN and IN (inferonasal)UP and OUT (superotemporal)
Body habitusMarfanoid (tall, thin)Marfanoid (tall, thin)
ThrombosisYES (homocysteine is prothrombotic)No
Intellectual disabilityYESNo
InheritanceAutosomal recessiveAutosomal dominant
DefectCystathionine β-synthaseFibrillin-1 (FBN1)
Treatment↓ Methionine diet, B₆, B₁₂, folateβ-blockers, aortic surveillance
💡 Step 1 Rule: Marfanoid habitus + lens subluxation + thrombosis + intellectual disability = homocystinuria, NOT Marfan. The NBME uses thrombosis and intellectual disability to distinguish them. Lens DOWN = homocystINuria (IN = INferior). Lens UP = Marfan (UP and OUT).

form31_page-134.title: Organophosphate Poisoning / Parathion
form31_page-134.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Cholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE + muscle weakness) + crop dusting chemical + treatment with atropine AND pralidoxime = organophosphate.

[45-year-old farmer + chemical spill + salivation + wheezing + diaphoresis + muscle weakness]
↓
Cholinergic crisis = excess ACh at muscarinic AND nicotinic receptors
↓
Treatment: atropine (muscarinic antagonist) + pralidoxime (regenerates AChE)
↓
Pralidoxime is specific for ORGANOPHOSPHATES (irreversible AChE inhibitors)
↓
NOT needed for carbamates (reversible inhibitors)
↓
Parathion = organophosphate insecticide used in crop dusting
↓
✅ D. Parathion

⚠️ USMLE Critical Distinction — Organophosphate vs. Carbamate:

FeatureOrganophosphate (Parathion)Carbamate (Carbaryl)
AChE inhibitionIRREVERSIBLE (phosphorylation)REVERSIBLE (carbamylation)
Pralidoxime needed?YES (regenerates AChE before "aging")NO (spontaneously reverses)
Atropine needed?YESYES
"Aging"Irreversible bond strengthens over timeDoes not age
SeverityMore severe, longer durationMilder, shorter duration

The SLUDGE mnemonic (muscarinic effects):

• Salivation
• Lacrimation
• Urination
• Defecation/Diaphoresis
• GI distress
• Emesis

Nicotinic effects (also present): Muscle fasciculations → weakness → paralysis, tachycardia

💡 Step 1 Rule: The NBME tells you the treatment includes pralidoxime — that's your confirmation it's an organophosphate (irreversible). If they only mention atropine, it could be either. Pralidoxime works by cleaving the organophosphate from AChE, but it must be given BEFORE "aging" (irreversible conformational change, ~24-48 hours).

BLOCK 4 — QUESTIONS 61–70

nbme28_q0096.title: Infective Endocarditis / Viridans Streptococci vs. S. aureus
nbme28_q0096.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Post-dental procedure + pre-existing valve disease + subacute presentation → viridans streptococci (e.g., S. mitis). The answer key lists S. aureus, but the classic Step 1 teaching for post-dental endocarditis on a damaged valve is viridans group streptococci.

[25-year-old + rheumatic mitral valve disease + root canal 1 month ago + fever + MR murmur]
↓
Subacute bacterial endocarditis
↓
Post-dental procedure on DAMAGED valve
↓
Alpha-hemolytic organism on blood agar
↓
Classic association: Streptococcus mitis (viridans group)
↓
Answer key states S. aureus — but note the Gram stain morphology matters:
↓
Clusters = Staph | Chains = Strep

⚠️ USMLE Historical Note: This is a controversial question. The traditional Step 1 framework:

Clinical ScenarioMost Likely OrganismHemolysis
Subacute endocarditis, post-dental, damaged valveViridans streptococci (S. mitis, S. sanguinis)Alpha
Acute endocarditis, IV drug use, normal valveS. aureusBeta
Prosthetic valve (<60 days post-op)S. epidermidisGamma/none
Prosthetic valve (>60 days post-op)Viridans streptococciAlpha
GI/GU procedureEnterococcus faecalisGamma/variable
Culture-negativeHACEK organisms, Coxiella, Bartonella—
💡 Step 1 Rule: For endocarditis questions, use the clinical tempo (acute vs. subacute) and risk factor (dental, IVDU, prosthetic valve, GI/GU procedure) to determine the organism. Alpha-hemolytic + post-dental + subacute = viridans strep. The Gram stain morphology (clusters vs. chains) is the tiebreaker if the vignette provides it.

nbme29_q0024.title: Minimal Change Disease / Normal Light Microscopy
nbme29_q0024.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Nephrotic syndrome in a child + normal glomerulus on light microscopy = minimal change disease.

[12-year-old + periorbital/dependent edema + hypoalbuminemia + proteinuria]
↓
Nephrotic syndrome in a child
↓
Biopsy: PAS-stained glomerulus appears NORMAL on light microscopy
↓
= Minimal change disease (MCD)
↓
EM would show: podocyte foot process EFFACEMENT
↓
IF negative
↓
Responds dramatically to CORTICOSTEROIDS
↓
✅ F. Minimal change nephrotic syndrome

⚠️ USMLE Historical Pattern: MCD appears on ~90% of NBME forms. The trap is picking FSGS (also causes nephrotic syndrome, but shows segmental sclerosis on LM) or membranous nephropathy (thickened capillary walls on LM).

Nephrotic Syndrome — Step 1 Glomerular Disease Decoder:

DiseaseAge GroupLight MicroscopyEM FindingIFTreatment
Minimal changeChildren (#1)NORMALFoot process effacementNegativeSteroids (excellent response)
FSGSAdults, African Americans, HIV, heroinSegmental sclerosisFoot process effacementIgM, C3 (focal)Steroids (variable response)
MembranousAdults (#1 primary)Thickened capillary wallsSubepithelial "spike and dome"Granular IgG, C3Anti-PLA2R Ab; rituximab
DiabeticDiabeticsKimmelstiel-Wilson nodulesGBM thickeningLinear IgGGlucose control, ACEi
AmyloidElderly, chronic diseaseCongo red (+), apple-green birefringenceFibrils—Treat underlying cause
💡 Step 1 Rule: Normal LM + nephrotic syndrome in a child = MCD. The NBME shows you a PAS-stained glomerulus that looks completely normal — that IS the diagnosis. If they showed you sclerosis, thickening, or hypercellularity, it would be something else. MCD = "minimal change" because you can't see anything wrong on light microscopy.

form30_page-125.title: Tinea Versicolor / Malassezia furfur
form30_page-125.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Hypopigmented/hyperpigmented macules on trunk + KOH prep showing "spaghetti and meatballs" = Malassezia furfur.

[27-year-old + hypopigmented patches × 2 years + worsened recently]
↓
Tinea versicolor
↓
Caused by Malassezia furfur (lipophilic yeast, part of normal flora)
↓
KOH prep: short hyphae + round spores = "spaghetti and meatballs"
↓
Inhibits melanin transfer → hypopigmented patches (more visible after tanning)
↓
Treatment: topical ketoconazole or selenium sulfide
↓
✅ C. Malassezia furfur

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students pick (E) Trichophyton — that causes tinea corporis/cruris/pedis (dermatophyte infections with annular, scaly, erythematous plaques). Tinea versicolor is NOT caused by a dermatophyte — it's caused by the yeast Malassezia.

Q64 · Concentric LVH / Sarcomeres in Parallel

What Step 1 is testing: Chronic pressure overload (hypertension) → concentric hypertrophy → sarcomeres added IN PARALLEL (wall thickens). Contrast with volume overload → eccentric hypertrophy → sarcomeres IN SERIES (chamber dilates).

Q65 · Fatty Acid β-Oxidation Defect / Hypoketotic Hypoglycemia

What Step 1 is testing: Hypoglycemia + NO ketones + dicarboxylic aciduria = fatty acid oxidation defect (MCAD or LCAD deficiency).

[6-month-old + unresponsive + glucose 20 mg/dL + urine dicarboxylic acids + NO ketones]
↓

Q66 · Testicular Cancer / Para-Aortic Lymph Node Drainage

Q69 · Metastatic Prostate Cancer / GnRH Agonist (Leuprolide)

What Step 1 is testing: Continuous GnRH agonist administration → pituitary desensitization → ↓ LH/FSH → ↓ testosterone → medical castration.

[68-year-old + metastatic prostate cancer → treatment?]
↓
Prostate cancer is androgen-dependent
↓
Goal: suppress testosterone
↓
GnRH agonist (leuprolide) given CONTINUOUSLY (not pulsatile)
↓
Continuous → desensitizes GnRH receptors → ↓ LH → ↓ testosterone
↓
= Medical castration
↓

What Step 1 is testing: Supplemental O₂ in premature neonates → disrupts VEGF gradient → abnormal retinal neovascularization → ROP. Maintaining O₂ sat 92-95% protects the retina.

↓
Premature retina is incompletely vascularized
↓

↓

↓
Neovascularization → hemorrhage → retinal detachment → blindness
↓
Careful O₂ titration protects the RETINA
↓
