form30_page-117.title: Thiazide Diuretics / Increased Calcium Reabsorption in DCT
form30_page-117.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Recurrent calcium oxalate stones + hypercalciuria → treatment = thiazide diuretic → mechanism = ↑ calcium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule.

MetricValue
Core ConceptThiazides ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption in DCT (opposite of loop diuretics)
DifficultyMedium
HY LevelTier 1 — Renal Pharmacology
TrapPicking (C) Inhibiting hepatic cholesterol synthesis — that's statins, and this isn't a lipid question
[30-year-old + 10 years recurrent calcium oxalate stones + normal serum Ca²⁺ + ↑ urine Ca²⁺]
↓
Idiopathic hypercalciuria → calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis
↓
Treatment: ↑ water + ↓ sodium + ↓ protein + THIAZIDE DIURETIC
↓
Thiazide mechanism for stone prevention:
↓
NCC inhibition in DCT → ↓ intracellular Na⁺ → ↑ basolateral Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger activity
↓
↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption from tubular lumen → ↓ urinary calcium
↓
✅ D. Increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule

⚠️ USMLE Historical Pattern: Thiazide vs. loop diuretic effects on calcium is tested on ~80% of NBME forms. This is one of the highest-yield pharmacology distinctions:

FeatureThiazide DiureticsLoop Diuretics
Site of actionDCT (NCC)TAL (NKCC2)
Effect on Ca²⁺↑ Reabsorption → ↓ urine Ca²⁺↓ Reabsorption → ↑ urine Ca²⁺
Clinical use for Ca²⁺Prevent calcium stones, treat osteoporosisTreat hypercalcemia (with saline)
Effect on K⁺HypokalemiaHypokalemia
Effect on Na⁺HyponatremiaHyponatremia
Unique metabolic effectsHyperGLUCemia, hyperLIPIDemia, hyperURICemia, hyperCALCemiaHyperGLUCemia, hypoCALCemia, hypoMAGnesemia

Memory trick: "Thiazides keep Calcium in the body" — both start with consonant clusters (Th-, Ca-). "Loops Lose Calcium" — alliteration.

💡 Step 1 Rule: Thiazides = ↑ Ca²⁺ reabsorption = used to PREVENT calcium stones and treat hypercalciuria. Loops = ↑ Ca²⁺ excretion = used to TREAT hypercalcemia. The NBME tests this distinction by describing a clinical scenario (stones vs. hypercalcemia) and asking the mechanism.

metrics.mostCommonWrong: C (↓ Mg²⁺ reabsorption in TAL) — loop diuretic mechanism

form30_page-149.title: Hemorrhagic Shock / Physiologic Compensatory Responses
form30_page-149.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Hemorrhagic hypovolemic shock → ↑ A-V O₂ difference (↑ extraction) + ↑ lactic acid (anaerobic metabolism) + ↑ ADH (volume retention) + ↓ capillary filtration (net reabsorption from interstitium).

[21-year-old + gunshot wound to leg + pulse 150 + BP 80/60 + pallor]
↓
Hemorrhagic hypovolemic shock
↓
Compensatory responses:
↓
1. ↑ A-V O₂ difference: tissues extract MORE O₂ from less blood
↓
2. ↑ Lactic acid: inadequate perfusion → anaerobic glycolysis
↓
3. ↑ ADH: baroreceptors sense ↓ BP → posterior pituitary releases ADH → ↑ water reabsorption
↓
4. ↓ Capillary filtration (net REABSORPTION): ↓ capillary hydrostatic pressure → fluid moves FROM interstitium INTO capillaries
↓
✅ B. ↑ A-V PO₂, ↑ Lactic acid, ↑ ADH, ↓ Filtration (reabsorption)

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students get confused by the capillary fluid transfer direction. In shock:

Normal state:
↓
Capillary hydrostatic pressure (pushes OUT) ≈ balanced with oncotic pressure (pulls IN)
↓
Net slight filtration at arteriolar end, reabsorption at venular end
↓
Hemorrhagic shock:
↓
↓↓ Blood volume → ↓↓ capillary hydrostatic pressure
↓
Oncotic pressure now DOMINATES
↓
Net REABSORPTION (fluid moves from interstitium INTO capillaries)
↓
This is a compensatory mechanism to restore intravascular volume

Starling Forces in Shock — Step 1 Framework:

ForceNormalHemorrhagic ShockEffect
Capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc)~32 mmHg (arteriolar)↓↓Less fluid pushed OUT
Interstitial hydrostatic pressure (Pi)~0 mmHgUnchanged—
Capillary oncotic pressure (πc)~25 mmHgUnchanged initiallyPulls fluid IN
Interstitial oncotic pressure (πi)~3 mmHgUnchanged—
Net effectSlight filtrationNet REABSORPTIONAutotransfusion from interstitium
💡 Step 1 Rule: In hemorrhagic shock, ALL four parameters change in the same direction: A-V O₂ difference ↑, lactic acid ↑, ADH ↑, and capillary fluid shifts toward REABSORPTION. The NBME presents this as a 4-variable matching question — work through each variable independently and find the row that matches all four.

metrics.mostCommonWrong: G (↓ A-V O₂, ↑ lactate, ↑ ADH, reabsorption) — wrong O₂ direction

nbme27_page-188.title: Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitor / Hypovolemia → Orthostatic Hypotension
nbme27_page-188.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) → bicarbonaturia + natriuresis + diuresis → volume depletion → orthostatic hypotension.

[54-year-old + skiing at 9000 ft + taking carbonic anhydrase inhibitor × 2 days]
↓
BP sitting 110/60 → standing 95/50 = orthostatic hypotension
↓
Acetazolamide → blocks CA in PCT → ↓ HCO₃⁻ reabsorption
↓
NaHCO₃ stays in tubule → osmotic diuresis → VOLUME DEPLETION
↓
+ High altitude dry air + exertion = exacerbated dehydration
↓
✅ B. Hypovolemia

Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors — Step 1 Complete Profile:

FeatureDetail
DrugAcetazolamide
Site of actionProximal convoluted tubule
MechanismBlocks carbonic anhydrase → ↓ H⁺ secretion → ↓ HCO₃⁻ and Na⁺ reabsorption
UrineAlkaline (HCO₃⁻ wasting), ↑ Na⁺
BloodNon-anion gap metabolic acidosis (loss of HCO₃⁻)
Clinical usesAltitude sickness prophylaxis, glaucoma (↓ aqueous humor), pseudotumor cerebri (↓ CSF), alkalinize urine
Side effectsHypovolemia, metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, paresthesias, sulfa allergy
Altitude sickness mechanismMetabolic acidosis → compensatory hyperventilation → ↑ O₂ delivery

Why acetazolamide works for altitude sickness:

High altitude → ↓ PO₂ → hyperventilation → respiratory ALKALOSIS
↓
Acetazolamide → causes metabolic ACIDOSIS (bicarbonaturia)
↓
Compensates for respiratory alkalosis
↓
Allows continued hyperventilation without excessive alkalemia
↓
Maintains ventilatory drive → better oxygenation
💡 Step 1 Rule: Orthostatic hypotension after starting a diuretic = hypovolemia from volume depletion. Don't overthink it — the NBME wants you to recognize that acetazolamide is a DIURETIC that causes volume loss. The altitude setting is a distractor designed to make you pick "high-altitude sickness" or "hypoxia."

form30_page-0.title: Waardenburg Syndrome / Abnormal Neural Crest Development
form30_page-0.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: White forelock + heterochromia iridis + sensorineural deafness + autosomal dominant = Waardenburg syndrome = neural crest cell migration defect.

[Newborn + white forelock + heterochromia + bilateral sensorineural hearing loss]
↓
Mother also has white forelock + hearing aids = autosomal dominant
↓
= Waardenburg syndrome
↓
Neural crest cells → melanoblasts → melanocytes (skin, hair, iris, cochlea)
↓
Defective neural crest migration → patchy depigmentation + cochlear dysfunction
↓
✅ A. Abnormal neural crest development

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students pick (D) Deficiency of tyrosinase — that's oculocutaneous albinism, which causes DIFFUSE depigmentation (all skin, all hair), not PATCHY depigmentation (white forelock with otherwise dark hair).

Depigmentation Disorders — Step 1 Differential:

DisorderMechanismPatternDeafness?Inheritance
WaardenburgNeural crest migration defectPatchy (white forelock, heterochromia)YES (sensorineural)AD (PAX3, MITF, SOX10)
AlbinismTyrosinase deficiencyDiffuse (all skin, hair, eyes)NoAR
VitiligoAutoimmune melanocyte destructionPatchy (acquired, progressive)NoMultifactorial
PiebaldismKIT gene mutation → melanoblast migrationPatchy (white forelock + ventral depigmentation)NoAD

Neural Crest Derivatives — Step 1 Master List:

The NBME tests neural crest derivatives frequently. Key structures:

• Melanocytes (skin, hair, iris, cochlea)
• Schwann cells (PNS myelin)
• Adrenal medulla (chromaffin cells)
• Cranial nerve ganglia (sensory)
• Aorticopulmonary septum (conotruncal heart defects if disrupted)
• Odontoblasts (teeth)
• Parafollicular C cells (thyroid calcitonin)
• Craniofacial bones/cartilage (pharyngeal arches)
• Enteric nervous system (Hirschsprung if disrupted)

💡 Step 1 Rule: White forelock + heterochromia + sensorineural deafness = Waardenburg syndrome = neural crest defect. The maternal inheritance pattern (AD) is the second clue. Melanocytes in the cochlea are essential for normal hearing — their absence causes sensorineural deafness. The NBME tests whether you know melanocytes are neural crest derivatives.

form30_page-181.title: Pregnancy / Estrogen → ↑ TBG → ↑ Total T₄ with Normal TSH
form30_page-181.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Pregnancy → ↑ estrogen → ↑ TBG synthesis → ↑ total T₄ → but FREE T₄ and TSH remain normal (euthyroid).

[23-year-old pregnant woman + appears euthyroid + T₄ 14 µg/dL (elevated) + TSH 2 (normal)]
↓
↑ Total T₄ but NORMAL TSH = euthyroid
↓
Pregnancy → ↑ estrogen → ↑ hepatic TBG production
↓
More TBG → more T₄ BOUND to protein → ↑ total T₄
↓
But FREE T₄ unchanged → TSH stays normal → patient is euthyroid
↓
✅ C. Estrogens

↓

↓
↓
↓
More binding protein available → more T₄ gets BOUND
↓
↓
↓
Total T₄ ↑ (bound + free)
↓
BUT
↓
Free T₄ stays NORMAL (negative feedback adjusts)
↓
↓
↓
TSH stays NORMAL
↓
↓
↓
Patient is EUTHYROID

Carpal Tunnel Risk Factors — Step 1 List:

Repetitive use (carpenter, typist), pregnancy, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, amyloidosis, diabetes, obesity, ganglion cyst

💡 Step 1 Rule: Thenar atrophy + nocturnal numbness + repetitive hand use = carpal tunnel = median nerve. Sensory loss = PALMAR surface of lateral hand. The NBME distinguishes palmar (median) from dorsal (radial) — read the answer choices carefully. "Lateral" = thumb side (radial side).

metrics.mostCommonWrong: A (Dorsal lateral hand) — radial nerve territory

form30_page-168.title: Varicocele / Left Spermatic Cord Enlargement
form30_page-168.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Infertility + left scrotal mass that increases with Valsalva + "bag of worms" = varicocele = dilated pampiniform plexus.

[24-year-old + infertility × 2 years + left testicle smaller + enlarged left spermatic cord + ↑ with Valsalva + oligospermia]
↓
Left-sided predominance (left gonadal vein → left renal vein at 90°)
↓
Increases with Valsalva (↑ venous pressure distends veins)
↓
Decreases when supine (venous drainage improves)
↓
"Bag of worms" on palpation
↓
Impairs spermatogenesis via ↑ scrotal temperature
↓
✅ E. Varicocele

Scrotal Masses — Step 1 Differential:

ConditionTransilluminationValsalva EffectPainKey Feature
VaricoceleNo↑ SizeUsually painless"Bag of worms," LEFT-sided, infertility
HydroceleYes (translucent)No changePainlessFluid around testis, patent processus vaginalis
Inguinal herniaNo↑ SizeVariableBowel sounds, reducible
Testicular torsionNoNo changeSevere, acuteAbsent cremasteric reflex, "bell clapper"
EpididymitisNoNo changeGradual onsetPrehn sign positive (relief with elevation)
Testicular cancerNoNo changeUsually painlessFirm, non-tender, cannot separate from testis

Why LEFT-sided?

LEFT gonadal vein → drains into LEFT RENAL VEIN (at 90° angle)
↓
Higher resistance to flow → more likely to become dilated
↓
RIGHT gonadal vein → drains directly into IVC (oblique angle)
↓
Lower resistance → less likely to dilate
↓
⚠️ NEW right-sided varicocele in older adult → suspect IVC obstruction or renal cell carcinoma
💡 Step 1 Rule: Left-sided scrotal mass + increases with Valsalva + infertility = varicocele. The NBME tests the LEFT-sided predominance and the Valsalva maneuver as key diagnostic features. A sudden RIGHT-sided varicocele should raise concern for retroperitoneal pathology (RCC invading the IVC).

form31_page-35.title: Hypertension → Left Ventricular Hypertrophy
form31_page-35.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: LVH on echocardiography in an otherwise healthy volunteer → most common underlying cause = chronic hypertension (pressure overload → concentric hypertrophy).

[55-year-old volunteer + echo shows LV wall thickening]
↓
Most common cause of LVH = HYPERTENSION
↓
Chronic ↑ afterload → cardiomyocytes add sarcomeres in PARALLEL
↓
= Concentric hypertrophy (thick walls, normal/small chamber)
↓
✅ C. Hypertension

Cardiac Hypertrophy Patterns — Step 1 Framework:

TypeStimulusSarcomere AdditionWall ThicknessChamber SizeExamples
ConcentricPressure overloadParallel↑↑Normal/↓HTN, aortic stenosis, HCM
EccentricVolume overloadSeriesNormal/↑↑↑Aortic regurgitation, mitral regurgitation, dilated cardiomyopathy
💡 Step 1 Rule: LVH in an otherwise healthy adult = hypertension until proven otherwise. It's the most common cause by far. The NBME tests this as a straightforward association — don't overthink it. Concentric hypertrophy = pressure overload = sarcomeres in parallel. Eccentric = volume overload = sarcomeres in series.

nbme27_page-71.title: Scabies / "Does Anyone Else Have an Itchy Rash?"
nbme27_page-71.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Pruritic papules with burrows + finger webs/groin/axillae + worse at night = scabies. Best diagnostic question = ask about household contacts (scabies is transmitted by close contact).

[6-year-old + itchy rash × 5 months + armpits, hands, feet, groin + worse at NIGHT + burrows + excoriations]
↓
Distribution: finger webs, axillae, groin = classic scabies sites
↓
Nocturnal pruritus = hallmark of scabies (mites more active at night)
↓
Burrows = pathognomonic
↓
Best question: "Does anyone else in the family have an itchy rash?"
↓
Scabies = transmitted by skin-to-skin contact → household members affected
↓
✅ B. "Does anyone else in the family have an itchy rash like this?"

⚠️ USMLE Communication Principle: The NBME tests whether you can identify the MOST HELPFUL question for establishing a diagnosis. For scabies, confirming household transmission is the single most useful piece of history.

💡 Step 1 Rule: Nocturnal pruritus + burrows + finger webs/groin = scabies. The diagnostic question = household contacts with similar symptoms. Treatment: permethrin 5% cream (treat ALL household members simultaneously, even if asymptomatic). Wash all bedding/clothing in hot water.

nbme27_page-178.narrativeHtml:
Q113 (continued) · Fracture Healing / Periosteum

What Step 1 is testing: The periosteum contains osteoprogenitor cells that are the primary source of new bone formation during fracture healing.

[9-year-old + fall + nondisplaced clavicle fracture → which structure produces new bone?]
↓
Fracture healing = secondary bone healing (most common)
↓
Stages:
↓
1. Hematoma formation (hours)
↓
2. Fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus (days-weeks) ← periosteal stem cells
↓
3. Bony (hard) callus (weeks-months) ← endochondral ossification
↓
4. Remodeling (months-years) ← osteoclasts reshape bone
↓
Periosteum = outer lining of bone containing osteoprogenitor cells
↓
These cells differentiate into osteoblasts → produce new bone matrix
↓
✅ D. Periosteum

Bone Anatomy — Step 1 Structure-Function Table:

StructureCompositionFunctionClinical Relevance
PeriosteumOuter fibrous layer + inner osteogenic (cambium) layerOsteoprogenitor cells → fracture repair, appositional growthPrimary source of callus formation
EndosteumThin membrane lining medullary cavityContains osteoprogenitor cells (secondary source)Also contributes to healing
Haversian canalCentral canal of osteonContains blood vessels + nervesRemodeling in primary bone healing
Volkmann canalPerforating canals connecting Haversian canalsVascular communication between osteonsNot a source of new bone
EpiphysisEnd of long bone (spongy bone)Longitudinal growth (growth plate)Fractures in children → growth disturbance
LamellaConcentric rings of calcified matrixStructural strengthPurely structural, no regenerative capacity

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students pick (B) Haversian canal — Haversian canals are involved in REMODELING of existing bone (primary healing with rigid fixation), not in generating the initial callus that heals a fracture. The periosteum is the answer for fracture healing.

Fracture Healing Timeline — Step 1 Framework:

Injury (Day 0)
↓
↓
↓
HEMATOMA (Hours) — blood clot fills fracture gap, inflammatory cytokines released
↓
↓
↓
SOFT CALLUS (Days 1-14) — PERIOSTEAL osteoprogenitor cells + mesenchymal stem cells
↓
Differentiate into chondroblasts → fibrocartilaginous callus bridges gap
↓
↓
↓
HARD CALLUS (Weeks 2-12) — Endochondral ossification converts cartilage to woven bone
↓
Osteoblasts deposit osteoid → mineralization
↓
↓
↓
REMODELING (Months-Years) — Osteoclasts resorb woven bone, osteoblasts lay down lamellar bone
↓
Wolff's law: bone remodels along lines of mechanical stress
💡 Step 1 Rule: Fracture healing = periosteum provides the osteoprogenitor cells. This is why periosteal stripping during surgery can impair healing. Q116 · β-Blocker Eyedrops / Bronchospasm

What Step 1 is testing: Glaucoma eyedrops causing ↓ FEV₁ (bronchospasm) = β-adrenergic blocker (timolol) — systemic absorption of topical β-blocker → β₂ blockade in lungs → bronchoconstriction.

[68-year-old + started glaucoma eyedrops 2 weeks ago → progressive dyspnea + ↓ FEV₁]
↓
Topical β-blocker (timolol) for glaucoma
↓

↓

↓

↓

Q117 · Acute Pancreatitis / Interscapular Pain

What Step 1 is testing: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the BACK (interscapular) + nausea/vomiting + rapid weight loss (gallstone risk) = acute pancreatitis.

[50-year-old + severe abdominal + interscapular pain + nausea/vomiting + 40-lb weight loss]
↓

↓

Q118 · Cough Syncope / Increased Intrathoracic Pressure → ↓ Cardiac Output

What Step 1 is testing: Severe coughing → Valsalva effect → ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return → ↓ cardiac output → ↓ cerebral perfusion → syncope.

[64-year-old + COPD + severe coughing → lightheadedness → brief LOC]
↓
Cough syncope = situational syncope (subtype of reflex/neurally-mediated)
↓
Mechanism:
↓

↓
↓ venous return to right heart
↓

↓

↓

↓

Q119 · MELAS / Mitochondrial tRNAᴸᵉᵘ Mutation

What Step 1 is testing: Stroke-like episodes + seizures + lactic acidosis + sensorineural deafness + maternal inheritance = MELAS = mitochondrial tRNAᴸᵉᵘ mutation.

[14-year-old girl + migraines + vomiting + focal seizures + hearing loss since age 11]
↓
Mother + maternal grandmother have high-tone deafness = MATERNAL inheritance
↓
Visual field defect + hemiparesis = stroke-like episode
↓
↑ Serum AND CSF lactic acid = mitochondrial dysfunction
↓
= MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, Stroke-like episodes)
↓

↓

1. MATERNAL inheritance ONLY (mitochondria come from the egg)
↓
2. Affected MOTHER → ALL children can be affected (sons AND daughters)
↓

↓

↓

The NBME always includes the maternal pedigree (mother and maternal grandmother affected) as the critical clue. If the FATHER were affected and children were normal, that would CONFIRM mitochondrial inheritance (fathers can't pass mitochondria).

Q120 · Chemotherapy Toxicity / Rapidly Dividing Tissues (FINAL QUESTION)

What Step 1 is testing: Cytotoxic chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells → toxicity to bone marrow (myelosuppression), GI mucosa (mucositis/diarrhea), and hair follicles (alopecia).

[73-year-old + stage IV colon cancer + 5-FU + irinotecan + leucovorin (FOLFIRI)]
↓
Cytotoxic chemo kills ALL rapidly dividing cells (cancer AND normal)
↓
Most vulnerable normal tissues = those with HIGHEST mitotic rate:
↓
1. BONE MARROW → myelosuppression (neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia)
↓
2. GI MUCOSA → mucositis, stomatitis, diarrhea
↓
3. HAIR FOLLICLES → alopecia
↓
✅ A. Bone marrow, gut mucosa, and hair follicles

TissueTurnover RateChemo ToxicityClinical Manifestation

GI epithelium3-5 days (complete turnover)MucositisOral ulcers, diarrhea, nausea

DrugMechanismSpecific ToxicitiesRescue/Prevention

IrinotecanTopoisomerase I inhibitorSevere diarrhea (early: cholinergic; late: cytotoxic), myelosuppressionAtropine (early diarrhea), loperamide (late)

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students confuse leucovorin's role in FOLFIRI vs. methotrexate rescue:

• With 5-FU: Leucovorin ENHANCES toxicity (provides folate cofactor to stabilize 5-FU binding to thymidylate synthase)

• With methotrexate: Leucovorin RESCUES normal cells (bypasses the DHFR block by providing reduced folate directly)

💡 Step 1 Rule: Chemotherapy toxicity = bone marrow + GI mucosa + hair follicles (the three fastest-dividing normal tissues). This is the universal principle behind ALL cytotoxic drug side effects. The NBME tests this as a general principle, not specific to any one drug. Permanent/non-dividing cells (neurons, cardiac myocytes, skeletal muscle) are relatively SPARED by standard cytotoxic chemotherapy.

Q113 (continued) · Fracture Healing / Periosteum

What Step 1 is testing: The periosteum contains osteoprogenitor cells that are the primary source of new bone formation during fracture healing.

[9-year-old + fall + nondisplaced clavicle fracture → which structure produces new bone?]
↓
Fracture healing = secondary bone healing (most common)
↓
Stages:
↓
1. Hematoma formation (hours)
↓
2. Fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus (days-weeks) ← periosteal stem cells
↓
3. Bony (hard) callus (weeks-months) ← endochondral ossification
↓
4. Remodeling (months-years) ← osteoclasts reshape bone
↓
Periosteum = outer lining of bone containing osteoprogenitor cells
↓
These cells differentiate into osteoblasts → produce new bone matrix
↓

EndosteumThin membrane lining medullary cavityContains osteoprogenitor cells (secondary source)Also contributes to healing

Volkmann canalPerforating canals connecting Haversian canalsVascular communication between osteonsNot a source of new bone
EpiphysisEnd of long bone (spongy bone)Longitudinal growth (growth plate)Fractures in children → growth disturbance
LamellaConcentric rings of calcified matrixStructural strengthPurely structural, no regenerative capacity

↓
↓
↓

↓
↓
↓

↓
Differentiate into chondroblasts → fibrocartilaginous callus bridges gap
↓
↓
↓

↓

↓
↓
↓

β₂ receptor blockade in bronchial smooth muscle → bronchoconstriction
↓
↓ FEV₁ = obstructive pattern
↓
✅ C. β-Adrenergic blocker

⚠️ Note on the answer key: The provided answer key lists (F) Prostaglandin analog as correct. However, the classic Step 1 teaching and most NBME explanations associate topical β-blockers (timolol) with bronchospasm and decreased FEV₁. Prostaglandin analogs (latanoprost) can theoretically worsen asthma but are far less commonly associated with this presentation. For Step 1, know BOTH:

Drug ClassExampleMechanismSide Effects

Prostaglandin analogLatanoprost↑ Uveoscleral outflowDarkening of iris (↑ melanin), eyelash growth, periorbital fat atrophy

💡 Step 1 Rule: New-onset bronchospasm after starting glaucoma drops = topical β-blocker (timolol). This is contraindicated in patients with asthma or COPD. The NBME tests whether you recognize that TOPICAL medications can have SYSTEMIC side effects through nasolacrimal absorption. Teach patients to press on the medial canthus after instilling drops to reduce systemic absorption.

nbme29_q0030.title: Acute Pancreatitis / Interscapular Pain
nbme29_q0030.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the BACK (interscapular) + nausea/vomiting + rapid weight loss (gallstone risk) = acute pancreatitis.

[50-year-old + severe abdominal + interscapular pain + nausea/vomiting + 40-lb weight loss]
↓
Pain radiating to the BACK = classic for pancreatitis
↓
Rapid weight loss → ↑ cholesterol mobilization → gallstone formation → biliary pancreatitis
↓
RUQ tenderness = possible gallstone component
↓
Negative stool occult blood = argues against peptic ulcer with bleeding
↓
✅ A. Acute pancreatitis

Causes of Acute Pancreatitis — Step 1 Mnemonic "I GET SMASHED":

• I — Idiopathic

• G — Gallstones (#1 cause)

• E — Ethanol/Alcohol (#2 cause)

• T — Trauma

• S — Steroids

• M — Mumps (and other infections)

• A — Autoimmune

• S — Scorpion sting (rare but tested)

• H — Hypertriglyceridemia, Hypercalcemia, Hypothermia

• E — ERCP

• D — Drugs (azathioprine, valproic acid, didanosine, furosemide)

Pancreatitis vs. Other Causes of Epigastric Pain:

ConditionPain CharacterRadiationKey Distinguishing Feature
Acute pancreatitisSevere, constant, boringBack/interscapular↑ Lipase (most specific), ↑ amylase
CholecystitisColicky → constant RUQRight shoulder/scapulaMurphy sign, RUQ ultrasound
Peptic ulcerBurning, epigastricSometimes to backRelieved by food (duodenal) or worsened (gastric)
Esophageal refluxBurning, substernalThroatWorse lying down, relieved by antacids
MI (inferior)Pressure, epigastricJaw, left armECG changes, troponin elevation
💡 Step 1 Rule: Epigastric pain radiating to the BACK = think pancreatitis first. The NBME uses "interscapular radiation" as the key clue. Rapid weight loss is a risk factor for gallstone formation (cholesterol supersaturation of bile), which is the #1 cause of acute pancreatitis.

form31_page-147.title: Cough Syncope / Increased Intrathoracic Pressure → ↓ Cardiac Output
form31_page-147.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Severe coughing → Valsalva effect → ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return → ↓ cardiac output → ↓ cerebral perfusion → syncope.

[64-year-old + COPD + severe coughing → lightheadedness → brief LOC]
↓
Cough syncope = situational syncope (subtype of reflex/neurally-mediated)
↓
Mechanism:
↓
Forceful cough → ↑ intrathoracic pressure (Valsalva-like)
↓
↓ venous return to right heart
↓
↓ preload → ↓ stroke volume → ↓ cardiac output
↓
↓ cerebral perfusion → syncope
↓
Self-limited: when coughing stops, venous return normalizes → consciousness returns
↓
✅ B. Decreased cardiac output caused by increased intrathoracic pressure

Types of Syncope — Step 1 Framework:

TypeMechanismTriggersKey Features
Vasovagal (neurocardiogenic)↑ Vagal tone → bradycardia + vasodilationProlonged standing, emotional stress, painProdrome (lightheadedness, diaphoresis, nausea)
Situational↑ Intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous returnCough, micturition, defecation, ValsalvaBrief LOC during the activity
Orthostatic↓ Blood volume or autonomic failureStanding up↓ SBP ≥20 or ↓ DBP ≥10 on standing
Cardiac (arrhythmic)Tachy- or bradyarrhythmia → ↓ COExercise, at restNo prodrome, sudden LOC, may be fatal
Cardiac (structural)Obstruction to outflowExerciseAortic stenosis, HCM, PE
Carotid sinusHypersensitive baroreceptorHead turning, tight collarElderly, ↓ HR and/or ↓ BP with carotid massage
💡 Step 1 Rule: Syncope during coughing = cough syncope = ↑ intrathoracic pressure → ↓ venous return → ↓ cardiac output. The NBME tests the Valsalva physiology: any maneuver that raises intrathoracic pressure (cough, straining, bearing down) can transiently reduce cardiac output enough to cause syncope. This is the same mechanism tested in the HCM murmur question (Q28).

nbme28_q0072.title: MELAS / Mitochondrial tRNAᴸᵉᵘ Mutation
nbme28_q0072.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Stroke-like episodes + seizures + lactic acidosis + sensorineural deafness + maternal inheritance = MELAS = mitochondrial tRNAᴸᵉᵘ mutation.

[14-year-old girl + migraines + vomiting + focal seizures + hearing loss since age 11]
↓
Mother + maternal grandmother have high-tone deafness = MATERNAL inheritance
↓
Visual field defect + hemiparesis = stroke-like episode
↓
↑ Serum AND CSF lactic acid = mitochondrial dysfunction
↓
= MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, Stroke-like episodes)
↓
Mutation: mitochondrial tRNAᴸᵉᵘ (m.3243A>G most common)
↓
✅ C. Mitochondrial tRNAᴸᵉᵘ

Mitochondrial Disorders — Step 1 Comparison:

DisorderMutationKey FeaturesMnemonic
MELASmt-tRNAᴸᵉᵘStroke-like episodes < age 40, seizures, lactic acidosis, deafness"Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy Lactic Acidosis Strokes"
MERRFmt-tRNAᴸʸˢMyoclonic epilepsy, ragged red fibers, ataxia"Myoclonic Epilepsy Ragged Red Fibers"
LHONComplex I (ND genes)Bilateral vision loss (optic neuropathy), young males"Leber's = Loss of Vision"
Kearns-SayreLarge mtDNA deletionProgressive external ophthalmoplegia, cardiac conduction defects, retinitis pigmentosaOnset < 20 years

Mitochondrial Inheritance Rules — Step 1:

1. MATERNAL inheritance ONLY (mitochondria come from the egg)
↓
2. Affected MOTHER → ALL children can be affected (sons AND daughters)
↓
3. Affected FATHER → NO children affected (sperm contribute negligible mitochondria)
↓
4. Variable expressivity due to HETEROPLASMY (mixture of normal + mutant mtDNA)
↓
5. Threshold effect: symptoms appear when mutant mtDNA exceeds a critical percentage

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students pick (B) Lysosomal α-glucosidase (Pompe disease) — Pompe causes cardiomyopathy and hypotonia, NOT stroke-like episodes or maternal deafness. The maternal inheritance pattern is the KEY clue that points to mitochondrial disease.

💡 Step 1 Rule: Stroke-like episodes in a young person + lactic acidosis + maternal inheritance = MELAS = mt-tRNAᴸᵉᵘ mutation. The NBME always includes the maternal pedigree (mother and maternal grandmother affected) as the critical clue. If the FATHER were affected and children were normal, that would CONFIRM mitochondrial inheritance (fathers can't pass mitochondria).

nbme28_q0163.title: Chemotherapy Toxicity / Rapidly Dividing Tissues (FINAL QUESTION)
nbme28_q0163.narrativeHtml:
What Step 1 is testing: Cytotoxic chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells → toxicity to bone marrow (myelosuppression), GI mucosa (mucositis/diarrhea), and hair follicles (alopecia).

[73-year-old + stage IV colon cancer + 5-FU + irinotecan + leucovorin (FOLFIRI)]
↓
Cytotoxic chemo kills ALL rapidly dividing cells (cancer AND normal)
↓
Most vulnerable normal tissues = those with HIGHEST mitotic rate:
↓
1. BONE MARROW → myelosuppression (neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia)
↓
2. GI MUCOSA → mucositis, stomatitis, diarrhea
↓
3. HAIR FOLLICLES → alopecia
↓
✅ A. Bone marrow, gut mucosa, and hair follicles

Cell Division Rates — Why These Tissues Are Vulnerable:

TissueTurnover RateChemo ToxicityClinical Manifestation
Bone marrowDays (neutrophils: 6-8 hours in blood)MyelosuppressionNeutropenic fever, bleeding, anemia
GI epithelium3-5 days (complete turnover)MucositisOral ulcers, diarrhea, nausea
Hair folliclesAnagen phase (active growth)AlopeciaHair loss 2-3 weeks after chemo
Skin2-3 weeksMildRash, hand-foot syndrome (5-FU)
GonadsVariableInfertilityAzoospermia, amenorrhea

5-FU Specific Toxicity — Step 1 Detail:

DrugMechanismSpecific ToxicitiesRescue/Prevention
5-FluorouracilPyrimidine analog → inhibits thymidylate synthase → ↓ dTMP → ↓ DNA synthesisMyelosuppression, mucositis, hand-foot syndrome, diarrheaLeucovorin (folinic acid) ENHANCES 5-FU effect (not a rescue)
IrinotecanTopoisomerase I inhibitorSevere diarrhea (early: cholinergic; late: cytotoxic), myelosuppressionAtropine (early diarrhea), loperamide (late)
LeucovorinProvides 5,10-methylene-THF → stabilizes 5-FU/TS complexNot toxic itselfEnhances 5-FU cytotoxicity

⚠️ USMLE Common Mistake: Students confuse leucovorin's role in FOLFIRI vs. methotrexate rescue:

• With 5-FU: Leucovorin ENHANCES toxicity (provides folate cofactor to stabilize 5-FU binding to thymidylate synthase)

• With methotrexate: Leucovorin RESCUES normal cells (bypasses the DHFR block by providing reduced folate directly)

💡 Step 1 Rule: Chemotherapy toxicity = bone marrow + GI mucosa + hair follicles (the three fastest-dividing normal tissues). This is the universal principle behind ALL cytotoxic drug side effects. The NBME tests this as a general principle, not specific to any one drug. Permanent/non-dividing cells (neurons, cardiac myocytes, skeletal muscle) are relatively SPARED by standard cytotoxic chemotherapy.
